July · Week 27

Independence Day Celebration 🎆

July 2 – July 8, 2027 · Days 183–189

Everything a party takes, Azlyn makes. A cake out of a cereal box on Friday, streamers on the scooter for Saturday, a real cake iced on Sunday morning and a bag packed for after dark. Monday onward the week runs on what July hands you: a paper vest she wears out of the house, ice melting on the path in six places, lunch she cuts herself, three dollar bills at the market.

Independence Day is Sunday and it gets the full day, from the parade round the block to the first fireworks either child has seen. Tuesday carries the other marker. The book is six months old, so the whole row of handprints comes off the wall, January to June, and a July one goes up beside them, with the same four questions underneath and her old answers read back to her. Kreston turns 13 months on Monday.

🧒 What Azlyn will learn
  • Cutting her own food. A butter knife through cucumber, tomato and cheese, and the different way each one gives.
  • Saying what she thinks will happen. Which ice cube goes first, how many seeds are in the watermelon, written down before anyone checks.
  • Counting past what she can hold. Flags on the street, candles onto a plate, watermelon seeds into a jar in tens.
  • Testing what she made and mending the part that failed. Three paper pockets, four objects, one stone that stayed in.
  • Three rules she can recite. She dictates the game rules for the fridge and the market rules in the car, then holds you to both.
👶 KRESTON THIS WEEK

Kreston is 12 months this week. He walks or is a week off it, drinks from a cup with both hands, and follows a one-step instruction. He turns 13 months on Monday the 5th, and from then he walks, climbs and carries things while he moves.

🌍 Around the world Week 27 · read it on Day 183

What Countries Eat on Their Big Day 🎂

Every country with a national day has a food attached to it. In Norway on the 17th of May the parade belongs to the children, and they eat ice cream and hot dogs all day. In India on the 15th of August families make candy in the orange, white and green of the flag. In Mexico on the 15th of September the dish of the night is chiles en nogada, which carries all three flag colors on one plate.

✨
Try it

Norway's answer is ice cream, and the children get it all day long. Have yours at the ten fifteen snack, outside and standing up, and tell her whose idea it was.

👩 What you'll learn
  • One-year-olds don't understand birthdays, and that's fine
  • Discovery requires an incomplete set
  • Pointing and giving are the foundations of conversation
  • Making something she wears is a different order of pride
  • Repeating an activity across seasons produces a comparison she can make herself
  • Involvement predicts eating better than persuasion does
  • Three rules, repeated forever, beats twenty rules said once
Did you know

Norway's national day parade has no soldiers in it at all. It is schoolchildren, from end to end.

Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

What a Party Needs

You need: 1 sheet of paper · crayons · her.

  1. Ask her what a party has to have. Write the list in her order, one thing per line, with a small picture beside each.
  2. Tell her the country has a birthday on Sunday and turns 251. Say the number twice and let her do what she likes with it.
  3. Circle everything on the list you could make out of a cereal box. Whatever she circled first is what you build at 9:15.

The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

The Cake That Never Gets Eaten

⏱️ 60 min🧰 6 items

You need: 1 cereal box or small shoebox, Colored paper, or plain paper and crayons, 1 roll masking tape, 1 pair of scissors (adult only), 1 pencil, for poking the candle holes, 1 permanent marker

  1. Tape the box shut along every seam and stand it on its end. She tapes, you hold the flaps down.
  2. She tears the colored paper up and tapes it over the box until no cardboard shows. Torn edges look like frosting. Plain paper gets crayoned first.
  3. Cut six paper strips, a hand long. She rolls each one round the pencil, slides it off and tapes it.
  4. Draw a flame on the top of each candle with the marker, then write 251 big on the side.
  5. Poke six holes in the top with the pencil where she points and stand a candle in each, loose enough to fall over.
  6. Sing to it. She blows, you tip the candles flat, she stands them back up. As many times as she asks.

💡Loose candles are the design. One that topples and goes back in gets blown at forty times before Sunday.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Counting the Flags on the Street

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Go before the heat and walk the streets with the most porches. Count flags: on poles, on porch rails, on car windows, in store doorways. Take her morning list and let her mark a line on the back for each one. She will want bunting to count, so let it count.

The Guest Who Doesn't Know It's a Party

Kreston has never been to a party. Azlyn throws him one, and she runs it.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: The cardboard cake, 6 paper cups, 1 small real snack: crackers, grapes cut lengthways, or berries, 1 blanket for the floor, 3–4 teddies, 1 phone, for the music

  1. She picks the room and spreads the blanket. Wherever it lands is where the party is.
  2. Teddies round the edge, Kreston in the ring with them. She hands out the six cups and decides who sits by who.
  3. Music on. She carries the cake in from another room and stands it on a low table at the edge of the blanket, back from the edge and where you can see it, while everybody watches her do it.
  4. Sing. She blows the candles down and stands them back up, and you sing again. Four rounds is not too many, and every candle that rolls off the table gets counted back into the cake before the next one.
  5. She shares the snack into the cups, one guest at a time, in the order she chose.
  6. She runs the dancing. The same song twice, and you on the floor for it.
  7. The party ends when she says. Cups collected in, cake up on the shelf where Kreston cannot reach the candles.

💡Sing and blow more than once. The part she is practicing is the ending, and a party that finishes four times gives her four goes at it.

Day 183 · For the grown-up A Birthday for a Country · Friday, July 2
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 12 months and walking or close to it. Stick a few loops of tape and a strip of colored paper to his tray and he will pull them off and wear them for a long while. Keep the rolled candles away from him, because they are the size he puts in his mouth. Let him walk part of the street holding one finger.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He is 12 months and drinks from a cup with both hands, so give him a paper cup with a splash of water and let him be a real guest. He will crawl into the middle and pull the cups over, and that is his part of it. Tell Azlyn that a guest who cannot talk yet joins in with his hands.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

One-year-olds don't understand birthdays, and that's fine.

Kreston has no idea the cake means anything. He reads the room instead: the singing, every face turned the same way, the pause before the clapping. Joint attention and anticipation are what a party gives a 12-month-old, and both are worth more to him this year than the idea of a birthday. Watch him look at whoever is loudest, then look at you to check whether loud is good. Azlyn is the one who needs today to mean something, so give her the running of it and give him the noise and the faces. He had his own turn a month ago, and he understood that one about as much as he understands this one.

⚠️

Safety: The scissors are adult-only and the paper strips are all they cut today, so put them back out of reach between cuts. The rolled candles are the width of Kreston's throat. Count six onto the cake and six off, and count them again after every blowing round at the party, because the cake sits on a table and he is on the blanket below it. Never leave one on the floor while he is down. Cut grapes lengthways. The flag walk runs in open sun, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you.

Cutting the Streamers

You need: 2 plastic grocery bags · 1 pair of scissors (adult only) · 1 roll masking tape.

  1. Cut the handles and the base off one bag so it becomes a tube. She holds it taut and pulls each strip free.
  2. Cut the tube round and round into strips a finger wide, then do the second bag. She says how long they get.
  3. Tape a bundle to a chair back and let her run past to see them lift. The best bundle goes on the front at 9:15.

Dressing the Scooter

⏱️ 60 min🧰 8 items

You need: Her scooter, balance bike, trike, or the stroller, The cut streamers, from two grocery bags, 1 roll masking tape, 2 clothespins, 5 playing cards, or pieces of cereal-box card, String, 3 feet, Crayons and paper, 1 pair of scissors (adult only)

  1. Tape streamers to both handlebar ends. She says how many go on each side, and she will want them uneven.
  2. Clip a peg to the frame by the back wheel with two cards in it so they clack as the wheel turns, and the same on the other side. On a stroller, clip them against the frame.
  3. Cut a rectangle of paper for the front. She draws her name on it and you tape it on.
  4. Tie the longest streamers to the back of the seat with the string. Nothing goes near the front wheel.
  5. Ride it up the hall. Listen for the cards, tighten the clothespins, tape down whatever flapped loose.
  6. Park it behind a closed door, or up out of Kreston's reach. It stays dressed until Sunday night.

💡Tape everything twice as much as looks necessary.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Test Lap

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Helmet on, and take the block at her pace with the stroller behind. This is a rehearsal, so let her stop every time a card comes loose. July mornings are warm by half ten: shaded side, and carry water.

The Museum with an Empty Shelf

The real museum is at 2:30. She opens her own first, and leaves one gap in it on purpose.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 5 items

You need: 1 shelf, windowsill or tray, 6–8 old objects: a coin, a photograph, a spoon, a key, a book, Paper cut into label cards, 8 of them, 1 marker, 1 roll masking tape

  1. Walk the house hunting for the oldest things in it, asking at each one: is this older than you? The wrong answers make the best conversations.
  2. Line them up on the shelf in her order, oldest first, and leave that order alone.
  3. She dictates a label for each one and you write her words on a card, including the ones that make no sense.
  4. Tape each card in front of its object. She reads the row back from memory, pointing as she goes.
  5. Leave one card blank and tape it at the end of the row. That one gets filled in at the museum.
  6. Take the blank card and the marker at 2:30. She draws the thing she liked best, standing in front of it.
  7. Tape it on the end of the shelf at home and let her give the tour again at bedtime.

💡Write the label in her words even where it is wrong. Spoon from the olden days when Grandad was a baby beats a correct date she never said.

Day 184 · For the grown-up The Parade She Can Ride In · Saturday, July 3
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 12 months and walking, or a week off it. He follows a one-step instruction now as long as the words never change, so carry the fifth playing card and hand it to him at every stop with the same four words: give it to Azlyn. He holds it out, waits for her hand, and wants another go the moment she takes it. His lidded cup rides in the stroller, because he drinks standing up with both hands on it. Keep every cut strip of grocery bag off the floor.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Take him in the carrier facing out. He gets the same job as this morning and the same four words: give it to Azlyn. Hand him her blank label card, let him pass it over, let her thank him. Twenty minutes is plenty.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Discovery requires an incomplete set.

A finished row of objects is a thing to look at. A row with one gap in it is a job. Azlyn will walk the museum hunting for the exhibit that fills her blank card, and she will look hard at forty things to choose one, which is far more looking than any instruction from you would buy. Bluma Zeigarnik found the same effect in waiters, who held unpaid orders in mind and lost them the moment the bill was settled. An open task stays live. Leave gaps on purpose: one empty page, one missing piece, one card nobody has written yet.

⚠️

Safety: Streamers near the front wheel will wrap and stop it dead, so check the front is clear before every ride. Helmet on, and stay between her and the road at every driveway. Cut grocery bag strips are a suffocation risk for a 12-month-old, so bag the offcuts now. Between rides the dressed scooter parks behind a closed door or up out of his reach, streamers, seat string and all. The coin and the key go above his reach. The test lap runs in full sun: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you.

Counting Out the Candles

You need: 1 box of birthday candles · 1 plate or tray.

  1. Tip the candles onto the tray and let her count them. Count them again together, touching each one.

The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

Two Hundred and Fifty-One Candles

⏱️ 60 min🧰 7 items

You need: 1 plain sponge, loaf cake, or 12 bought buns, 1 tub of cream, cream cheese or thick yogurt, 1 pint of strawberries and 1 pint of blueberries, 1 blunt knife and 1 spoon, The birthday candles she counted out, 1 plate or tray, Matches or a lighter (adult only)

  1. Cake onto the tray. She spoons the cream on and spreads it with the blunt knife. Lumpy is correct.
  2. Pull the green tops off the strawberries and let her slice them. Fruit gives under a blunt knife and she needs to feel that.
  3. Stripes of strawberry across the cake with cream showing between them, blueberries in a square in the top left. She places every berry.
  4. She pushes her candles in wherever she wants them, including all in one corner.
  5. Light them once now, sing, and let her blow. Blow out the rest yourself and put the matches back up high.
  6. Stand it beside Friday's cardboard cake and photograph the pair. One gets eaten tonight and one does not.

💡Into the fridge the moment it is photographed. July does bad things to cream on a counter.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Parade Round the Block

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take the block at her speed with the stroller behind, the scooter still dressed and the cards rattling. Wave at anyone on a porch, because on the Fourth they wave back. Go before eleven and carry water.

Second main event · 1:00–2:30 PM

The Bag for After Dark

Tonight she stays up past dark for the first time she will remember, and the afternoon goes on getting ready.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 8 items

You need: 1 rucksack, 1 picnic blanket, 1 flashlight with fresh batteries, Snacks and 1 lidded cup, Ear defenders, or cotton balls and a woolly hat, 1 sweater each for Azlyn and Kreston, 1 favorite toy, Paper and crayons

  1. Spread everything on the floor and let her see the pile before anything moves. Name each thing and what it is for.
  2. She packs the rucksack herself, one item at a time. Blanket at the bottom, sweaters on top, snacks and the cup where she can reach them.
  3. Test the flashlight. Let her work the switch thirty times, and tell her the flashlight is her job tonight.
  4. Ear defenders on, and talk to her through them so she hears what they do. With cotton balls, tuck it under the woolly hat.
  5. Agree a hand signal for too loud and practice it ten times, you first, then her. She gives it tonight and you leave, no discussion.
  6. She draws what she thinks fireworks look like before she has seen any. It goes in the bag and comes out tomorrow.
  7. Talk the spot through: where you sit, how far the car is, where the toilets are. The toy goes in last.

💡Say the leaving plan out loud before you go, and mean it. A three-year-old who knows she can go home will last twice as long as one who suspects she is stuck.

Day 185 · For the grown-up The Fourth of July · Sunday, July 4
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 12 months. Let him push the empty stroller down the flat stretch with both hands on the bar, which takes him further than he walks alone. Quarter his strawberries lengthways and halve the blueberries.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He is 12 months and has never heard a firework. Put the ear defenders on him for a minute at a time this afternoon so tonight is the second time and not the first. Plan on him asleep against you by the second bang.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Pointing and giving are the foundations of conversation.

Kreston hands you things all day and points at what he cannot reach. Both are him starting a conversation with no words in it: he has something in mind and he wants your attention on it. Packing the bag hands him fifty chances at it. He picks the flashlight up, holds it out, waits for you to take it. Answer every offer out loud with the name of the thing. Babies who point and give a lot at twelve months tend to have bigger vocabularies at two. He chooses, you name, and the word arrives attached to something he cared about first. He will hand you the same sweater five times. Take it the fifth time like the first.

⚠️

Safety: Lit candles come nowhere near a walking one-year-old. Put Kreston in the high chair before the matches come out, not on your hip. If there are sparklers tonight they stay in adult hands, and they stay hot long after they go out, so have water to drop them in. July heat is the real risk: water every half hour whether she asks or not, and the parade is an hour of open sun, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. If the paddling pool comes out, Kreston stays within arm's reach of you every second it holds water, and you tip it out before you go back in. Before dark, photograph what she is wearing and write your phone number on her arm.

The Paper Bag Vest

⏱️ 60 min🧰 5 items

You need: 1 large paper grocery bag, or brown parcel paper, or a large cereal box flattened, 1 pair of scissors (adult only), Crayons or felt tips, 1 roll masking tape, The three lengths of string from this morning

  1. Flatten the bag with the base at the top. Lay the shoulder-to-knee string down the front so she sees where the bottom edge lands.
  2. Cut a neck hole in the base panel and an arm hole in each side, sizing them with the arm string. Cut them bigger than looks right.
  3. Cut straight up the middle of the front, bottom edge to neck hole, so it opens like a vest. Try it on her.
  4. Run masking tape round the neck and both arm holes. Paper tears at a hole first, and taped edges get this thing to Thursday.
  5. The table is hers now: both sides, inside included, every crayon she wants. No paint today and nothing wet.
  6. She wears it out at half ten and she wears it to dinner.

💡Cut it a size too big, so she can get it on without you.

Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Walking on the Shady Side

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Cross to whichever side of the street has the trees and stay on it. Put her hand flat on a wall in the sun, then on one in the shade, and let her tell you the difference before you name it. Work out where that shade will be by four.

Pockets That Hold Things

The vest has nowhere to put anything, and she has a stone she wants to keep.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: The vest, Paper, card, and 3 old envelopes, 1 roll masking tape, 4 test objects: 1 stone, 1 spoon, 1 crayon, 1 toy car, 1 marker, 1 pair of scissors (adult only)

  1. Cut the top off an envelope and tape it to the front of the vest on three sides, top left open. That is pocket one.
  2. She loads it with the stone, then walks, jumps, spins and runs the hall. Watch which bit of tape lets go first.
  3. Fix that bit and nothing else, then send her round again with the same stone.
  4. Pocket two comes from folded paper and pocket three from card. She picks the shapes and where they go, including the back.
  5. Test all three with all four objects, one at a time. She marks a tick or a cross on each pocket with the marker.
  6. Count the ticks. Whichever shape carried the stone is the one she wants three of, so cut the extras and tape them on.
  7. Load every surviving pocket and let her walk the hall with all four objects on her.

💡Let the bad pocket fail the whole way. Reinforcing it before she tests it saves the envelope and costs her the information.

Day 186 · For the grown-up The Day After · Monday, July 5
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston turns 13 months today. He walks, climbs and carries at the same time now, so fold a square of leftover bag paper into a pad too big to fit in his mouth and let him ferry it from one end of the room to the other. Say happy thirteen months out loud, because nobody else will.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

At 13 months he climbs onto whatever is knee height, and the woods are full of things at knee height. Let him do the low log with a hand held rather than carrying him past it. Azlyn will want him in a vest too, so tape a spare pocket to his shirt.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Making something she wears is a different order of pride.

She will stop the mail carrier to show him the vest, and she will ask to sleep in it. Azlyn builds her sense of herself out of two things: what she can do, and what belongs to her. A thing she made that then sits on her body lands in both piles at once, which a drawing on the fridge never manages. Expect her to defend it from Kreston harder than she defends any toy, because the toy came from a store and this came out of her hands. Let her wear it out of the house, creased and torn, all week.

⚠️

Safety: The scissors come out three times today. Put them on a shelf between cuts, not on the arm of the sofa. The stone and the toy car are choking size for a 13-month-old who walks over and picks things up, so count the four test objects back into a bowl at the end. If the afternoon goes to the stream or the paddling pool, Kreston stays within arm's reach of you every second he is near the water, and you tip the pool out before you go in. Shade takes the heat off and leaves the burn, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you.

Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

Six Chalk Circles

You need: Chalk · 6 saucers or jar lids.

  1. Go out before the heat and ask her for six places that differ: full sun, deep shade, grass, the doorstep, a dark stone, the wall.
  2. She stands a saucer down at each one, and you draw round it in chalk and number the circles one to six.
  3. Ask which circle will empty first. Write her answer on the path in chalk and leave it where you can both read it later.

The Ice That Won't Last

⏱️ 60 min🧰 7 items

You need: 2 trays of ice cubes, frozen overnight, Chalk, The 6 saucers or jar lids, already out on the circles, 1 dish towel, 1 bowl of warm water, The kitchen clock, or a timer on your phone, Paper and 1 marker, for the results

  1. Carry one tray out under the dish towel. She puts a cube on each saucer in number order, drying her hands between them.
  2. Write the time at the top of the paper and set the timer for ten minutes.
  3. Check all six at every buzz. She calls out which are shrinking and you write it down against the numbers.
  4. Between checks, give her the bowl of warm water and a spare cube from the second tray. That one vanishes in a minute and keeps her out there.
  5. Write 1st, 2nd and 3rd on the paper as each circle empties, and let her be the one who calls it.
  6. Read her eight o'clock prediction back to her at the end, and chalk a tick beside it if she called it right.

💡Ten minutes is a long time at three. Set the timer where she can press it herself and give her the chalk between buzzes.

Today the shade under them is a different temperature from the sidewalk, and she can stand with one foot in each. Take the photo from the January spot.

Her Hand Next to January's

January's handprint went up on Day 1 and one has gone up every month since. July's makes seven of twelve, made the same way, with the same four questions under it.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: The six handprint sheets from January onward, or the photos of them, Washable non-toxic poster paint, 1 wide soft brush, 1 wet washcloth in a shallow bowl, Thick paper, 3 sheets, 1 marker

  1. Get all six earlier sheets out first and lay them in a row, January at one end. Ask whether any of those hands looks like her hand, and let her hold her palm over January's and over June's.
  2. Paint her palm with the brush rather than dipping it. Press flat, count to three, lift straight up onto the thick paper.
  3. Washcloth in your hand before she lifts, and wipe her down where she stands.
  4. Do Kreston's beside hers on the same sheet while he is calm.
  5. Write July and the date under both prints with the marker. Seventh of twelve. The six earlier sheets go back up on the wall in order, and the new one tapes up at the end of the row.
  6. Ask the four questions from Day 1 again and write her answers word for word on the second sheet: favorite color, favorite food, favorite song, what she wants to do this year.
  7. Read her January answers back to her after. She will disagree with herself, which is the best part of it.

💡She will want a second print. Let her, on the third sheet, and get the first one out of reach before she improves it.

Day 187 · For the grown-up Ice in July · Tuesday, July 6
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months. Keep the ice cubes away from him. Set the bowl of warm water on the grass in front of him and let him slap it. He will carry the empty saucers to you one at a time if you ask.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He comes to the pool too, and a hand stays on him from the changing room to the water every time, including the two steps to the bench. At 13 months he walks, and poolside is the worst floor in the building for a new walker. In the pool he wants to be upright and moving, so the shallow steps are where he will spend the hour. Keep him inside arm's reach the whole time and get him out before he goes cold.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Repeating an activity across seasons produces a comparison she can make herself.

Azlyn will put her palm down on January's outline without being asked, and the gap round the edge of it is the whole lesson. One handprint is a keepsake for you. Seven, made the same way across seven months, are evidence she can read without being told what to think. Same paint, same brush, same four questions, same size of sheet, so the only thing that changed is her. Keep the method identical every time, even where you can see a better way to do it, because a bigger sheet or a different paint gives her a difference she cannot pin on herself. By December she will guess the gap before the paint comes out.

⚠️

Safety: Ice cubes are a choking hazard for a 13-month-old and half of them end up on the ground, so count them out and sweep before he is down. The warm-water bowl at nine and the bowl of water at quarter past four are standing water at his height, so Kreston stays inside arm's reach of you while either one is full, and you tip them out when she has finished. Swimming needs eyes on both children for the whole hour, both of them inside arm's reach, and the phone stays in the bag. July sun burns faster than it feels: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

Pulling the Husks Off

You need: 2 corn on the cob · 1 large bowl · 1 saucepan.

  1. Give her both cobs and the bowl and let her strip the green husks off. Show her once, then leave her with it.
  2. The silk is the long job. Every thread comes off, and she will hunt them for twenty minutes.
  3. Stand the bare cobs in the saucepan of cold water on the back of the stovetop, ready for noon.

Everything She Can Cut with a Butter Knife

⏱️ 60 min🧰 7 items

You need: The 2 husked corn on the cob, 1 cucumber, 2 tomatoes, 1 block of cheese, 1 loaf of bread, 1 pot of yogurt, 1 lemon, olive oil, salt, 1 butter knife and 1 chopping board, 2 bowls and 1 serving plate, 1 saucepan, for the corn

  1. Cucumber onto the board first, because it gives without a fight. Show her one cut, hand over the butter knife, and step back. Cut pieces go into a bowl as she works.
  2. Tomatoes next. The skin resists and then goes all at once, and she needs to feel that. Cheese in slabs, bread torn.
  3. Dip: yogurt into a bowl, half the lemon squeezed in, a spoon of oil, a pinch of salt. She stirs, tastes, and says what it needs.
  4. Corn onto the stovetop at twenty past eleven, so the water is boiling by half past and the cobs have their ten minutes before noon. You stand at the pan, she stays the other side of the counter.
  5. She lays the whole lot out on the serving plate however she wants. Say nothing about the arrangement.
  6. It goes on the table at noon and nobody rearranges it, including you.

💡Cucumber, tomato, soft cheese and bread all give way to a butter knife. Banana and boiled egg will do the same job next week.

What's Ripe on This Street

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

July is the month the street starts producing. Walk it looking at what is growing where: tomatoes going red in pots, blackberries still hard and green, apples the size of marbles, zucchini under leaves. Ask which ones you could eat today. If a neighbor is out, let her ask them.

One Whole Watermelon

One watermelon takes the whole afternoon: weighed, guessed at, opened, counted, eaten outside.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 7 items

You need: 1 whole watermelon, 1 large knife (adult only), 1 spoon each, 1 large bowl and 1 tray, Kitchen scales, if you have them, 1 jar with a lid, for the saved seeds, Chalk, or paper and a crayon, for the guesses

  1. Let her lift it first. Weigh it on the scales, or pass it round and see who holds it out longest. Write the weight in chalk.
  2. Guesses: how many seeds are in it? Write hers, write yours, put one down for Kreston. Nobody changes their answer later.
  3. Cut it on the tray with her standing back where she can see, and put the big knife out of reach before anyone touches a piece.
  4. Everyone eats outside, spoons only, seeds spat onto the tray. This mess hoses off.
  5. Count the seeds into the jar in tens, out loud, and let her decide whose guess was closest.
  6. Lid on the jar and onto the windowsill. Those get planted in the spring.
  7. Fill the bowl at the tap and float the rind halves in it. They sit like boats and she will push them round until dinner.

💡Let her spit the seeds. The tray catches all of it.

Day 188 · For the grown-up Azlyn Makes Lunch · Wednesday, July 7
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and wants to be at the counter with everyone else. Give him the thick end of the cucumber, too big to choke on and cold on gums that are working hard this month, and let him gnaw it in the high chair beside her. Hand him the empty bowl to carry after.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He gets watermelon scraped to a mush with a spoon, no chunks and no seeds near him. At the library, put him down in the board book corner and let him pull books off the low shelf. He will bring one back to you over and over, so take it every time and read the first page.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Involvement predicts eating better than persuasion does.

The cucumber she cut is a cucumber she eats. Children who handle, wash, cut and serve food eat more of it and try new things sooner. Handling wears the strangeness off, and she has had this cucumber in both hands since a quarter past nine. By noon she has smelled the lemon, felt the tomato give under the knife and tasted the dip twice while stirring, so what arrives at the table is a known thing that belongs to her. Say nothing about eating it. A three-year-old who made lunch and is then encouraged to eat it hears pressure instead of an invitation.

⚠️

Safety: The big knife is adult-only, it cuts the melon once, and it goes back out of reach before anybody eats. Watermelon chunks and seeds are choking size for Kreston at 13 months, so his portion gets scraped to a mush. The rind bowl, the afternoon dishpan and the paddling pool if it comes out are standing water at his height, so Kreston stays within arm's reach of you whenever any of them is full, and you tip them out the moment she has finished with them. The corn pan is boiling water at her head height: handle turned in, and she stays the other side of the counter while it is on. Kreston goes in the high chair for the twenty minutes the pan is up, because the corn runs through free play and he walks. The street walk is forty-five minutes of July sun, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

What Makes It a Game

You need: 1 ball · a clear bit of floor.

  1. Play a game she knows, rolling the ball between you, and stop halfway through on purpose.
  2. Play it again with no rules for one minute: ball anywhere, score whenever you like, both at once. Let it get daft and let her complain.

The Game That Goes on the Fridge

⏱️ 60 min🧰 5 items

You need: 1 piece of card, or the back of a cereal box, 1 marker, Chalk, 1 ball, Masking tape, or 1 fridge magnet

  1. Ask her to invent a game and let it run long and mad. Take every rule she says, including the ones about dragons.
  2. Play it once through as she described it. It falls apart somewhere, and that collapse is the material for the hour.
  3. Cut it down to three. Say them back as a list: you have to do this, you can't do that, this is how you win. Let her correct you until it matches.
  4. Write the three rules on the card in marker, with a picture beside each so she can read them back without you.
  5. Take the chalk out and mark what the game needs on the ground: a start line, a target, a place to stand.
  6. Tape the card to the fridge at her height. It stays there for the summer and anyone can play it.

💡Write her words, not the tidy version. A rule she can recite is a rule she will enforce on you at dinner.

Take the chalk and the ball to the biggest flat surface you can reach on foot and draw the game out full size: the line, the target, a box for each player. Play it five times, and anyone walking past gets asked to join.

The Money in Her Own Pocket

The market is at two thirty and she is going in with three dollar bills that belong to her and a list she can read.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 5 items

You need: Paper and crayons, for the picture list, 3 one-dollar bills, 1 small purse, an envelope, or the vest pocket, 1 shopping bag she can carry herself, 1 marker

  1. Decide together what she is buying. Three things, and she draws each one on the paper however she likes.
  2. Write the word beside each drawing in marker, so a stallholder can read it over her shoulder if she goes shy.
  3. Count the three bills into her hand, then into the purse. Open and shut it ten times, because a purse she fumbles gets handed to you.
  4. Agree the three market rules out loud in her words: hold the bag, hands off the fruit unless we are buying it, stay where you can see me.
  5. Rehearse the asking. You be the stallholder, four times, until can I have one please comes out without a run-up.
  6. She packs the bag herself: the list, the purse, nothing else.
  7. At the market she hands the money over and takes the change back into her purse while you stand behind her.

💡Let her count the money out at her own speed and let the line wait.

Day 189 · For the grown-up Three Rules · Thursday, July 8
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months, walks, and carries things while he moves, which makes him a useful ball fetcher. Give him that job out loud and let Azlyn be the one who hands it to him. If she wants one of the three rules to be about him, write it down.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Keep him in the carrier or strapped into the stroller at the market. At 13 months he points at everything he wants and he can reach a fruit display from a stroller, so park side-on. Name what he points at every time, even the fortieth.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Three rules, repeated forever, beats twenty rules said once.

Azlyn holds about three pieces of information at a time, and a loud market takes that down to two. Twenty careful instructions in the car are gone before the door shuts. The card on the fridge works for the same reason the market rules do: three items, the same words every time, a picture she can read without you. She will start reciting them at you, correcting your version, enforcing them on Kreston, and the rule leaves your mouth for good. Resist the fourth. Each one you add pushes another out, and the one that falls off is never the one you would have chosen.

⚠️

Safety: Her change comes back as coins, and a coin is a choking hazard for a 13-month-old who walks over and picks things up, so the purse lives in her pocket or your hand and every coin goes straight back into it. The market means traffic, a crowd and a curb: say the three rules before you get out of the car, not on the sidewalk, and keep a hand on the stroller brake while she pays. The full-size game runs on open ground at half past ten, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

Day 190
Float It or Sink It
The Big Book of Little Days · July · Week 27Day 189 · for the grown-up
July · Week 28

Beach & Water Fun 🏖️

July 9 – July 15, 2027 · Days 190–196

Water is the material all week. Azlyn floats things and sinks them, moves a bucket of it across the yard by sponge, sends it down five bottle chutes taped to the fence, and paints a wall the sun wipes clean behind her. The same question comes back in a new form every day: what does water do, and what makes it stay where you put it? By Thursday she has a fleet of boats, a sea sealed in a bottle, four name stones and a beach she built in the yard.

No holiday lands this week, so the heat is the thing to plan around. Monday is the longest stretch outdoors of the seven days and wants shade, a hat and a drink she can reach without asking. Saturday's sand goes under a trash bag and comes back out on Wednesday, Friday's boats sail again in the paddling pool on Thursday, and the salt water on Tuesday takes half an hour in the sun to show what it did. Nothing she makes gets thrown out before the week is finished.

🧒 What Azlyn will learn
  • Shape decides what floats. One square of foil sinks as a ball and carries a cargo of pasta as a boat.
  • Water is what makes sand hold. Dry sand slumps out of the cup, damp sand keeps its corners, and one pitcher too many turns the lot to soup.
  • The long out-breath, down a straw, under a feather, and up at a paper spiral that only turns for a slow one.
  • Pouring, aiming and squeezing with pitchers, sponges, a squeezy bottle and chutes she moves herself until the water lands where she wants it.
  • That she can finish a job she can see. Grubby pile on her left, clean row on her right, and she works from one side to the other.
👶 KRESTON THIS WEEK

Kreston is 13 months this week. He walks, climbs, and carries things while he moves, which in a week of water means he carries it. He gets his own cup, his own sponge and his own end of the towel every day, and he stays within arm's reach of anything full.

🌍 Around the world Week 28 · read it on Day 190

Australia: Swim Between the Flags 🏖️

Australian beaches carry two flags in the sand, a red and yellow pair at each end of a stretch of water. The water between them is the part the lifesavers are watching, and children there learn the phrase before they can swim. The flags move up and down the beach as the currents shift, so the safe patch is never in the same place twice.

✨
Try it

Push two red and yellow paper flags into the grass and let Azlyn set the safe water. Eat fairy bread between them: white bread, butter and a heavy shake of sprinkles, cut into triangles.

👩 What you'll learn
  • Same material, different shape, opposite result
  • Open-ended materials outperform toys, and cheap ones outperform expensive ones
  • Slow exhalation is the body's own calming switch
  • Give three tools and let her choose
  • Visible results are what sustain a child's effort
  • Competition at three works when everyone wins something real
  • Historical injustice, explained plainly, does not damage a three-year-old
Did you know

Surf Life Saving Australia has over 180,000 members, and most of the people on patrol are volunteers.

The Float Pile and the Sink Pile

You need: 1 dishpan half filled with water · 8 small things from the kitchen · 1 dish towel.

  1. Let her pick them: a spoon, a cork, a lid, a peg, a craft stick, a bottle cap. Nothing that matters if it gets wet.
  2. One at a time, and she calls it before she drops it. Sinkers on the dish towel, floaters beside it.

The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

Ball, Boat, Same Foil

⏱️ 60 min🧰 8 items

You need: 1 roll kitchen foil, 1 dishpan or clear storage box, 1 pitcher of water, Dried pasta, a handful, or 20 coins as cargo, 1 permanent marker, Paper and a pen for her guesses, 2 old dish towels, 1 plastic cup and 1 shallow tray for Kreston

  1. Tear two squares of foil the same size, a hand span each, and lay one on the other so she sees they match.
  2. Scrunch the first into a tight ball. Press the second over your fist and pinch the sides up into a boat.
  3. Write her guesses on the paper before either touches the water: ball, floats or sinks; boat, floats or sinks.
  4. Spread the dish towels, stand the bowl on them, fill two-thirds and mark the water level with the marker. Both shapes go in at once, one in each hand.
  5. Give the boat a cargo: five pieces of pasta, one at a time. It sits lower in the water and stays up, while the ball lies on the bottom carrying nothing.
  6. Now she builds the boat and you do nothing. Hers comes out a different shape, floats anyway, and the result goes on the paper under yours.

💡Drop them together rather than one after the other. She will ask you to flatten the ball out and try again.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Leaf Boats Down the Gutter

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take a two-liter bottle of water to the top of a driveway or a dead-end stretch, well back from any through road; July gutters are bone dry. Pour a slow stream into the curb channel and send leaves down it, one each. They snag on grit and stop dead, and she kneels on the sidewalk side to clear the channel with her fingers. Save the last of the bottle for the drink she forgets to ask for.

Four Boats and a Wave

The bowl stays where it is and the fleet gets bigger: four boats out of the recycling.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 8 items

You need: Kitchen foil, 1 empty margarine or ice cream tub, 6 plastic bottle caps, 6 craft sticks, Paper for sails, 1 sheet, 1 roll masking tape, 2 drinking straws, The bowl of water from this morning

  1. Four piles along the table: foil, the margarine tub, the caps, the sticks. She builds one boat from each and you keep your hands off three.
  2. Foil goes over your fist again. The margarine tub is a boat already. Five craft sticks tape side by side into a raft, the sixth upright in the middle.
  3. The six caps tape rim to rim into a block, two rows of three.
  4. Tear four rough sails. Tape a straw mast into the foil boat and another into the tub, a sail to each. The raft's sail goes on its standing stick; the cap boat's folds into an L and tapes flat.
  5. Float all four at once and ask which boat the wave will beat.
  6. One hand each side of the bowl, rock it once. That is the wave. Watch what tips, then rock harder.
  7. Keep going until one boat is left upright. Mend the sunk ones and sail again.

💡Hand her the bowl for the last few waves and let her decide how hard.

Day 190 · For the grown-up Float It or Sink It · Friday, July 9
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and carries things while he walks. Give him his own cup and a shallow tray with a finger of water in it at the far end of the towels. He fills the cup, walks three steps, tips it and goes back for more. He runs that loop for five minutes, wanders off, and comes back to it across the morning.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

At 13 months he climbs, and a dishpan on the floor is a thing to climb into. Sit him beside it with the margarine tub boat, mast pulled out, the one thing in the fleet too big to go in his mouth. He bangs the surface flat-handed to make his own wave.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Same material, different shape, opposite result.

Two identical squares of foil went into the same water and did opposite things. Azlyn cannot hold the density explanation at three and she does not need it. She keeps the rule underneath: the same stuff arranged two ways behaves two ways. Children this age work out physical rules by watching one thing change while everything else stays still, and you set that up for her by tearing the squares the same size. She will ask why the boat floats. Answer with another test. Flatten the ball out, fold it into a third shape and put it back in the water.

⚠️

Safety: Standing water. Kreston is 13 months, he walks, and he can drown in the depth of a dishpan in silence. He stays within arm's reach whenever it is full, and the bowl gets tipped the moment they stop. Torn foil scraps, pasta, corks, lids and bottle caps all go straight in his mouth, so keep the offcuts on the table and sweep before you put him down. The gutter run puts her hands at the edge of a live road, so stay between her and the road, and Kreston rides in the stroller with the brake on or holds your hand with the road on your side of him. July sun burns before it feels hot: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

Stand the dishpan on two old dish towels by the back door with the foil and the marker. Buy a bag of play sand today; tomorrow runs on it.

Raiding the Kitchen Drawer

You need: the kitchen drawer · 1 basket · the towel in the yard.

  1. Hand her the basket and two rules: nothing sharp, nothing that plugs in.
  2. She chooses six things she thinks could shape sand. Let the daft ones through; a potato masher beats anything sold as a sand tool.

The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

Wet Sand, Dry Sand

⏱️ 60 min🧰 6 items

You need: 1 bag play sand (substitute: dry garden soil, or a bag of rice for the dry half only), 1 large storage box or dishpan, 1 pitcher of water, 1 metal spoon, 1 sieve, 2 cups, 1 ice cube tray, 1 potato masher, 1 old towel underneath, 1 dustpan brush

  1. Box on the towel, dry sand two hands deep, tools along the edge.
  2. Dry first. She fills both cups and the ice cube tray, turns them out and watches it slump. Sieve it, spoon it, pile it up.
  3. Half a pitcher of water into one end. Mix it with the spoon and let her get her hands in. Fill a cup and turn it out; somewhere in that pitcher the sand starts holding.
  4. Press a flat patch with the potato masher and let her stamp a print in it. Fill the ice cube tray and turn out blocks that keep their corners.
  5. The rest of the pitcher goes in until it turns to soup. Ask her where it went wrong; dry sand from the far end is the repair.
  6. Sweep the spills back into the box with the dustpan brush.

💡Let her ruin it in step five. She has to see the soup to know that wet has two ends.

The Train to the Seaside

Four dining chairs in a line down the hall, and the 2:30 train is a real one.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 7 items

You need: 4 dining chairs, Paper for tickets and a sign, 2 sheets, 1 marker, 1 hole punch, or 1 pair of adult scissors (adult only), 1 roll masking tape, 1 bag, 1 towel and 1 book to pack, 1 saucepan lid as the whistle

  1. Chairs in a line, two and two, all facing the same way. The front one is the driver's and she picks who sits there.
  2. Fold a sheet of paper into six, write SEASIDE on each panel with the marker and tear them apart into tickets.
  3. She punches a hole in every ticket, or you snip a corner off each with the adult scissors.
  4. The second sheet is the destination sign. She tells you the word, you write it, and it tapes to the front chair.
  5. Pack the bag together: the towel, the book, and whatever else she says a person needs at the sea.
  6. Everyone boards and hands over a ticket. Bang the saucepan lid for the whistle and pull out.
  7. She calls the stops, you say what goes past the window, and the last stop is the sea.

💡Keep two tickets back for the real train at 2:30. She hands one to an actual guard.

Day 191 · For the grown-up Wet Sand Holds · Saturday, July 10
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and he will eat a handful of sand before you finish turning round, so he gets his own end of the towel and his own cup with a splash of water in it. Barefoot on grass is worth five minutes on its own at his age. He stands still and looks down at his feet.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He rides too. At 13 months a moving train is hard work, all vibration and strangers and things sliding past the window, so a short hop out and back is plenty. Sit him on your lap facing the glass and name three things as they go.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Open-ended materials outperform toys, and cheap ones outperform expensive ones.

A bag of play sand costs less than takeout and held her for twenty minutes at a stretch, three separate times before lunch. Sand has no finished state, so nothing she does to it counts as wrong, and she will take risks with it she would never take with a puzzle that has one right answer. She wrecked the wet sand on purpose to find where the edge was. Researchers who time children's play find the longest stretches over materials with no built-in outcome: sand, water, dough, blocks. The toy with a button and a song does one thing well, and she has finished it by Tuesday. Buy the sand.

⚠️

Safety: Sand in eyes, and sand in Kreston's mouth. Play sand only, never builder's sand, and keep it damp so it cannot blow about. The box stays at her end of the towel and he stays at the other end with his own cup. If it gets in her eyes, rinse with clean water and no rubbing. Four surfaces in the open take her out of the shade, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you.

Choosing the Blue

You need: 3 clear glasses of water · blue food coloring · 1 teaspoon · a bright window.

  1. One drop of coloring in the first glass, three in the second, six in the third. She counts them in and stirs each with the teaspoon.
  2. Hold all three against the window: a swimming pool, the sea on a good day, the sea in a storm.
  3. She picks the one that goes in the bottle at 9:15. Leave that glass at the front of the counter.

The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

The Sea in a Bottle

⏱️ 60 min🧰 6 items

You need: 2 clear plastic bottles, 500 ml, labels peeled off, Cooking oil, about 1 1/4 cups (300 ml), Blue food coloring, 1 funnel (substitute: the top third of a third bottle, cut off), 1 roll packing tape for sealing the lid, 1 pitcher of water

  1. Fill each bottle a third of the way from the pitcher. Add the blue she chose, counting the drops out loud, then cap and shake until the color is even.
  2. Funnel in the neck. Pour the oil in slow, half the bottle each, stopping a hand's width from the top.
  3. Lid on tight, neck wiped dry, then two full turns of packing tape over the lid and down onto the shoulder. This lid does not come off again.
  4. Lay it flat and lift one end, slow as you can. One wave travels the whole length and slows when you do.
  5. Now let her shake it as hard as she likes. Everything breaks into beads. Set it down and wait two minutes for the layers to find each other again.
  6. The second bottle is hers from the start, you holding the funnel and saying nothing.

💡Check the tape before you hand it over, and again next week. A leaking bottle is a cupful of oil on the carpet.

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

What One Breath Can Move

A blowing station goes up on the kitchen table.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 8 items

You need: 4 drinking straws, 10 cotton balls, 1 feather, or a torn strip of tissue, Tissue paper or paper towels, 3 sheets, Paper for the spinner, 1 sheet, 1 pair of adult scissors (adult only), 1 roll masking tape, 1 ping-pong ball, or a scrunched foil ball

  1. Two lines of masking tape down the table a hand's width apart, three feet long. That is the track, with a strip across each end.
  2. A cotton ball each at the start line, a straw each, and blow them down the track. Race three or four times and let her win some.
  3. Swap in the ping-pong ball. Heavier, slower, and it wants a long steady blow rather than a hard puff.
  4. The feather comes off the table. She keeps it up with her mouth alone and you count out loud until it lands.
  5. Tear the tissue paper into squares. Hold one flat on the wall, blow at it and take your hand away. It hangs a second or two.
  6. Cut a spiral out of the paper yourself, from the outside in. Tape a loop of masking tape to the middle and hang it from a shelf edge.
  7. Blow up at the spiral. A hard puff swings it about. One long slow out-breath turns it round and round.

💡Keep the spiral. Leave it hanging, and on the afternoons that fall apart at four o'clock, take her over and both of you blow.

Day 192 · For the grown-up The Slow Wave · Sunday, July 11
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and this bottle is built for him. Once the tape is on, let him have it on the grass. It is heavy enough to be interesting, it rolls, and the blue keeps moving after he has stopped. He will carry it around the yard and bring it back to Azlyn.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Cotton balls and a 13-month-old do not mix, so he gets the sealed bottle and the far end of the room. At the playground he wants the steps rather than the slide, so let him have the ladder with your hands hovering.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Slow exhalation is the body's own calming switch.

Azlyn spent the afternoon on a breathing exercise and nobody mentioned breathing. The out-breath is the half of the cycle that slows the heart. A long exhale raises vagal tone and takes her off the accelerator. The paper spiral turns for a long steady stream of air and swings about for a hard puff, so she had to slow down to make it go round. Telling a wound-up three-year-old to take a deep breath fails; she gulps the air in and holds it. Give her something to move with her mouth and the long breath arrives on its own: a straw, a feather, birthday candles, bubbles in a glass.

⚠️

Safety: Cotton balls, the ping-pong ball and loose straws all fit down Kreston's throat. Count them out and count them back in before he is on the floor, and keep the whole station at the far end of the table. Flat on a towel in the shade they both still burn, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you.

The Painting the Sun Takes Back

⏱️ 60 min🧰 8 items

You need: 1 bucket of water, 1 wide house-painting brush (substitute: a dish brush), 1 large sponge, 1 empty squeezy bottle, rinsed, 1 stick of chalk, 1 pitcher for refilling, A fence or shed side, and one dry paving slab, 1 small sponge and 1 plastic cup for Kreston

  1. Bucket at the foot of the fence in what shade there is, pitcher beside it.
  2. Brush first. She paints a long stripe along the fence and the beginning has gone by the time she reaches the end.
  3. Sponge next, pressed flat on the shed door in whole prints. Count how long each lasts; the ones in shade hold longer.
  4. She lays a hand on the paving, you paint round it, then chalk the outline before it vanishes. The water goes, the chalk ghost stays.
  5. Squeezy bottle, filled from the pitcher. Squirting a line high up the wall is the best thing all morning; give it twenty minutes.
  6. Last one is a race. She paints a shape at one end of the fence and runs to the other end and back before it dries.

💡Keep the bucket in shade and top it up from the pitcher. A trip indoors to the tap ends the whole thing.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Hot Wall, Cool Wall

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take her round the outside of the house with one hand out, touching as she goes. The sunny wall, the shaded wall, the paving, the grass, the car hood (your hand first, always). July gives the biggest spread of the year. Finish in the coolest spot she found and have the drink there.

🎨 MAKE
Second main event · 1:00–2:30 PM

The Water Wall on the Fence

Five bottles get taped to the fence with a bucket at the bottom.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 7 items

You need: 5 plastic bottles, mixed sizes, 1 craft knife or heavy scissors (adult only), 1 roll parcel or duct tape, A fence, shed side or wall (substitute: a large flattened box propped against a wall), 1 pitcher and 1 bucket, 1 dishpan to catch, 1 plastic cup for Kreston

  1. Cut the bottles into open chutes while she stands back: bottom off, one long side out, lid left on. Tape every cut rim twice round; the edges come out sharp.
  2. Knife away on a shelf. She picks where the first chute goes and you tape it at her angle.
  3. Pour a pitcher in the top. Flat chutes hold onto it, steep ones throw it clear over the next.
  4. Let her move it. One chute, one change, one pitcher, and the answer arrives in four seconds.
  5. Add the second and third chutes so the water lands in each in turn. Bucket at the bottom, bowl under the worst leak.
  6. All five up. She pours the whole pitcher in and you watch how much arrives in the bucket.
  7. Tip the bucket back into the pitcher and run it again. Leave the wall up.

💡Use about twice as much tape as looks necessary. A chute that peels off mid-pour costs you ten minutes.

  • Two chutes, one bucket, and stop there.
  • Float bottle caps down the run and see which make it.
  • Tape the chutes to the side of the bath and do it indoors.
🌳 Out again · pick one
  • A green space with a ball, kept to the shaded half of the field
  • The park with the big trees, for a picnic tea underneath them
  • The riverside path, a few degrees cooler than the street
  • The playground after five, once the metal has come off the boil
Day 193 · For the grown-up Water on the Wall · Monday, July 12
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and copies whatever Azlyn is holding, so give him his own small sponge and a cup with an inch of water. He paints the paving by dropping the sponge and picking it up. Check the ground with your hand before you set him down in bare feet.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He is 13 months and carries things while he walks, so the water wall hands him a real job: filling his cup at the bucket and delivering it to the top chute. It arrives half empty. Take it, pour it in and tell him what it did. Out with the ball he chases it and falls over it.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Give three tools and let her choose.

Three is the number that works inside a single job. One tool at the fence is an instruction. Ten tools for one wall stall her, and she stands there holding nothing. Three lets her compare, pick and change her mind inside a minute, and the picking is the part that kept her at the fence past the twenty minutes you expected. Choice inside limits you set is the whole trick: you decided it was water on the wall, she decided it was the squeezy bottle. Researchers looking at autonomy find children given a real choice within a set task stay longer and argue less. Setting out three things instead of one costs you nothing.

⚠️

Safety: Heat. This is the longest stretch outdoors all week, so shade, a hat, cream at eight, cream again at eleven, and a drink she can reach without asking. Cut bottle edges are sharp, so tape every rim before it goes on the fence and check them with your thumb. A full bucket in the sun is standing water with a 13-month-old beside it, so tip it the moment you finish. The knife and the scissors stay with you, on a shelf between cuts.

The Two-Bowl Car Wash

⏱️ 60 min🧰 7 items

You need: 2 dishpans, Warm water and a squirt of dish soap, 1 old toothbrush, 1 sponge, 1 nail brush, 2 old towels, 1 length of string and 6 pegs for the drying line, The trike, the rain boots, the plastic animals and the dolls from the pile, 1 small bowl, 1 sponge and 1 plastic animal for Kreston

  1. Tie the string between the fence and a chair leg at her knee height, low enough that no loop reaches anybody's neck, and hang the clothespins along it. That is the drying line.
  2. Bowl one gets warm water and a squirt of liquid, bowl two clean water for rinsing. Her dirty line on the left, an empty towel on her right.
  3. Three brushes, one demonstration each and then hands off: toothbrush for wheels and joints, nail brush for rain boot soles, sponge for the big flat sides.
  4. Wash, rinse, then peg or lay out. Doll clothes on the line, the trike and the rain boots on the towel to drip.
  5. Halfway down the pile, look at bowl one. The water is gray. Tip it on the plants and mix a fresh one.
  6. Stand back at the end and look left, then right. Nothing on her left, a full row on her right.

💡She will wash the same wheel for eleven minutes. Leave her on it.

Painting With Sea Water

Six spoons of salt in a jar of warm water make a paint that shows nothing for half an hour.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: Table salt, 6 tablespoons, 1 jam jar of warm water, 1 spoon, Dark paper, 2 sheets (substitute: brown parcel paper, or a flattened cereal box colored dark with a crayon), 1 paintbrush, A sunny windowsill

  1. Six tablespoons of salt into the jar of warm water. She counts them in and tips each one.
  2. Stir with the spoon until the salt stops disappearing. The last of it sits on the bottom; the water is full.
  3. Brush loaded, she paints on the first sheet of dark paper. It looks like wet paper, so tell her the sun finishes it.
  4. Flat on the sunny windowsill and leave it. Go and do something else for half an hour; standing over it makes the wait worse.
  5. Come back. White lines have come up out of nowhere, following every stroke her brush made.
  6. Second sheet, bigger and wetter: her name, a handprint, the sea. Back on the sill.
  7. Hold the dry one to the light and let her rub a line with one finger. The crystals come off on her skin.

💡Warm water takes about twice the salt that cold water will. Start the jar hotter rather than stirring more salt into cold.

  • The splash pad, if the pool line is round the block

Day 194 · For the grown-up The Toy Wash · Tuesday, July 13
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and copying chores is starting in earnest. Give him a small bowl with an inch of water, one sponge and one plastic animal, on the towel where you can see him. He washes it the way he has watched Azlyn wash hers: in and out forty times. Stay within arm's reach of every bowl.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He goes in too. At 13 months he walks on land, and the pool floor is all drag and no grip, so both your hands stay on him. Twenty-five minutes, out while he is enjoying it, food within the half hour. Let Azlyn show him how to slap the surface.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Visible results are what sustain a child's effort.

The grubby pile on her left shrank and the clean row on her right grew, and she could check her own progress without asking you. A three-year-old cannot hold an abstract goal for forty minutes, and she does not have to when the evidence sits in front of her in two lines. Effort follows visible change at this age, which is the reason she abandons tidying her bedroom: a room halfway through looks the same as a room she has not started. Set a job up so the work leaves a mark she can see. Clipping washing, filling a jar, laying the table.

⚠️

Safety: Two full bowls at Kreston's exact height, and he walks now. Mix the water warm rather than hot, keep the soapy bowl at the back out of his reach, and tip both the moment she finishes. Soap in the eyes ends the morning, so the rinse bowl stays clean. Run the drying line at knee height and never at her chest, because a line at her chest is at Kreston's neck, and take it down once the last thing is dry. The wash runs on open paving: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

A Stone for Every Player

  1. Hunt four flat stones from the yard or the pot plants, one for every person in the house. She chooses whose is whose.
  2. Wash them in the bowl and dry them on the cloth. Wet stones will not take a marker.

Moving the Sea by Sponge

⏱️ 60 min🧰 8 items

You need: 4 buckets or dishpans, 1 shallow tray for Kreston, an inch of water in it, 3 sponges, 1 stick of chalk for the lines, 1 pitcher, 1 towel, 1 phone timer, The name stones

  1. Chalk a start line and a finish line as far apart as the garden allows. Grass between them if you have it.
  2. Two buckets on the start line, filled from the pitcher and from the tap. Two empty ones on the finish line, a name stone in front of each.
  3. A sponge each, and one rule that never bends: nobody may carry a bucket.
  4. Two minutes on the phone timer. Soak, run, squeeze, run back. Towel on the finish line for wet feet.
  5. Stop dead on the timer and look. Tip the first finish bucket into the pitcher, mark the level with your thumb, empty it, then do the second and see whose comes higher.
  6. Round two, and she changes one thing: two sponges at once, a bigger sponge, a longer timer, both hands.

💡Play it for real. Run, drop things, lose. A three-year-old spots a grown-up going easy on her from a long way off.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Chalk Sea You Jump Into

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Chalk a wide wavy sea across the paving with three or four islands in it, big enough to land both feet on. The rules are hers. Jump island to island, and whoever lands in the sea goes back to the start. Draw a shark in the gap she finds easiest. It washes off in the first rain, which in this heat means September.

Best Castle, Best Door, Best Moat

Three bowls of yesterday's damp sand, three builders, and three prizes named before anybody starts.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: The damp sand from Saturday, split between 3 bowls, 1 pitcher of water, 3 spoons and 3 cups, 3 paper flags on craft sticks or straws, plus masking tape to fix them, The name stones, A phone for the photographs

  1. Three bowls out on the grass, one each, name stone on the rim of each.
  2. Say the three prizes out loud now, before a single handful gets moved: Best Castle, Best Door, Best Moat.
  3. Pitcher on the grass for topping up; sand that dried out overnight needs a splash before it holds.
  4. Build for as long as it runs, twenty minutes or forty. Cups as molds, spoons for digging the moat and cutting the door.
  5. Tear three paper triangles for flags, tape one to a craft stick each, and everyone plants theirs when they are finished.
  6. Judge it out loud and hand out all three prizes. Say what won each one and mean it.
  7. Photograph the three castles side by side with the name stones in front, then let her flatten hers.

💡Build a trash castle yourself. She spends half the time watching what you are doing, and a wonky door gives her room to make hers her own way.

Day 195 · For the grown-up Beach Games in the Garden · Wednesday, July 14
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and gets the third sponge. He will not run it anywhere useful; he carries it across the grass, drops it, picks it up and sets off again. His own shallow tray with an inch of water in it goes at the far side, clear of the racing, so the sponge has somewhere to go. Never leave him beside a full bucket while you are timing a round.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He gets the third bowl of sand and no prize he understands. At 13 months he climbs, so at the play center the low soft steps are where he wants to be rather than the ball pit. Follow him up them. Say happy building to him when the flags go in.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Competition at three works when everyone wins something real.

Azlyn is old enough to want to win and too young to take a loss without the afternoon ending. Three-year-olds have started measuring themselves against other people, which is the reason she ran so hard this morning, and their sense of fairness runs well ahead of their ability to absorb coming second. Naming the three prizes before anyone builds keeps the wanting and takes out the wreckage. She hears three real categories, picks one to aim at, and wins a thing she chose in front of the whole family. Losing well arrives around five or six on its own schedule, and an afternoon where everybody wins something real costs her nothing while she waits.

⚠️

Safety: Wet paving and running feet. Run the game on grass where you have it, and on paving everybody walks the course rather than runs it, with the finish buckets standing on a towel. The buckets stay full for the length of one game and get tipped between rounds, because Kreston will head straight for them the second the shouting starts. Sand goes in eyes at the castles, so rinse with clean water and no rubbing. Water into both of them every half hour, hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

Everybody in the Pool

The pool goes up on the flattest ground you have and everyone gets in.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 7 items

You need: 1 paddling pool (substitute: 2 large storage boxes, or the bath), Warm water, mixed by pitcher from the kettle and the tap, 2 pitchers, 4 cups and 1 colander, The fleet of boats from Friday, The sea bottle from Sunday, 1 towel each, Sun cream and hats

  1. Pool on the flattest, shadiest spot within reach of the tap. Rinse it and let it warm through for twenty minutes.
  2. Fill it cold from the tap. Sit Azlyn and Kreston down on the grass at the far side, and carry the two pitchers of hot water out only once they are both down. Stir them through with your arm and test it with your own elbow.
  3. Now everyone gets in. You first, Kreston on your lap, and Azlyn watches her mother sit in a paddling pool in her clothes.
  4. Pitchers and cups first: pour over shoulders, fill, tip, fill again. The colander held over a head makes rain.
  5. Friday's fleet comes in, all four boats sailing round three people's knees.
  6. Sunday's sea bottle goes in last. She tips it end over end under the surface and watches one wave run the length of it while the whole thing floats.
  7. Lunch on the towels and the afternoon out there. Sun cream again once everyone is dry.

💡Get in. She has spent a week doing water at arm's length in bowls and buckets.

Day 196 · For the grown-up The Beach at Home · Thursday, July 15
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and carries things while he walks, so give him the bag to hold between finds and let him drop each one in himself. Anything smaller than his fist goes into your pocket rather than his hand. He will want to sit down on the warm sidewalk, so put the back of your hand on it first.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

At 13 months he can sit in two inches of warm water and stay busy for five or ten minutes at a stretch, coming back to it across the afternoon, and he will try to stand up every four minutes. Keep a hand on him. He gets a cup of his own, and on the errand he walks the last stretch holding one finger.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Historical injustice, explained plainly, does not damage a three-year-old.

Everyone in your house got in the water today. In America, public pools and beaches were closed to Black families inside living memory, which is why whole generations there were never taught to swim and why the drowning-rate gap still sits where it does. Azlyn reads a hesitation as a rule about what may be said, so say it without the flinch: there was a time when some people were kept out of the water because of their skin, that was wrong, and people changed it. Say it once, answer the follow-up, let her get back in. She may hand it back to you wrong next week. Correct it in one sentence and leave it there.

⚠️

Safety: The paddling pool is the real hazard of the week. Kreston is 13 months and walks, so he is within arm's reach every second it holds water and it is never left filled while you go indoors. The kettle stays in the kitchen, and the hot water crosses the garden only while both children are sitting down at the far side. Everything after nine runs outdoors: hat on, cream at nine, cream again at eleven, and once more after the pool.

Day 197
Ice Cream Without a Freezer
The Big Book of Little Days · July · Week 28Day 196 · for the grown-up
July · Week 29

Ice Cream & Summer Treats 🍦

July 16 – July 22, 2027 · Days 197–203

Everything this week is cold and she makes most of it herself. Friday she shakes cream and salted ice in a bag for ten minutes and eats the result out of the bag. That afternoon five ice cubes go into five wrappings, and she opens all of them every twenty minutes to see which one is still there at dinner. Thursday runs the same idea long: a fork dragged across a freezing tray every half hour from half past nine in the morning.

Between those two ends the week turns outward. She marks where the hatch goes in a big box on Saturday, you cut it, and she serves you from behind it. She builds a sundae to everybody's order on Sunday, and freezes a pot for each person on Monday with the flavor picked from something she has noticed about them. Tuesday the stroller becomes a van and the whole house moves when she rings and stops when she stops. Wednesday she names eight people who did something for her this week and rolls each name inside a paper cone. Nothing lands on the calendar, so the heat sets the shape: kitchen in the morning, shade or water after lunch.

🧒 What Azlyn will learn
  • Salt makes ice colder than ice. She shakes a bag of cream buried in salted ice and eats ice cream out of it ten minutes later.
  • What keeps cold in. Foil, a dish towel, shredded paper in a lidded box, a bowl of water, bare on a saucer. She predicts first, then checks every twenty minutes.
  • Waiting, counted down. Eight pegs come off a string one at a time while the granita freezes, so half an hour turns into something she can see.
  • Taking an order and giving change. She runs the hatch of a cardboard shop, hands out the jobs, then swaps sides and lines up as the customer.
  • Saying what she has noticed about a person. Four frozen pots and eight paper cones, each carrying one name and one reason in her own words.
👶 KRESTON THIS WEEK

Kreston is 13 months this week. He walks, climbs anything with a lip on it, and carries things from room to room while he moves.

The Big Book of Little Days · JulyWeek 29 · opener →
🌍 Around the world Week 29 · read it on Day 197

Frozen Treats Everywhere 🍧

People ate frozen candy long before anyone had a freezer. Iranian cooks made faloodeh, thin frozen noodles in rose water and lime, from ice kept underground all summer in a yakhchāl. Sicily has granita, Mexico sells paletas from street carts, and Japan shaves ice into a soft mountain called kakigōri.

✨
Try it

Squeeze half a lemon into a cup of apple juice, freeze it and scrape it with a fork. That is granita, and Azlyn makes a tray on Thursday.

  • Celebration is a legitimate way to teach history
  • Children describe parents by what they do, not who they are
  • Food is the most durable carrier of family memory
  • Admiration is how children choose which traits to grow
  • Moving in time with someone builds connection, measurably
  • Gratitude needs a target before it needs a feeling
  • Waiting is easier when it's visible and shrinking
Did you know

Persian ice houses were built 2,400 years ago and kept ice through desert summers.

Filling the Cold Bag

You need: 1 large zip-seal freezer bag · a tray of ice cubes · 6 tbsp table salt · 1 tablespoon · masking tape and a marker.

  1. She loads ice into the big bag by the handful until it is half full. It sticks to wet fingers and she will refuse help.
  2. Six tablespoons of salt go in on top. She spoons, you count out loud.
  3. Seal it, tape a strip across the front and write COLD BAG on it. Tell her the salt is doing something to that ice, and she finds out at 9:15.

Ten Minutes of Shaking

⏱️ 60 min🧰 10 items

You need: 1 small zip-seal sandwich bag, 1 large zip-seal freezer bag (from 8:00), 2/3 cup heavy cream or whole milk (150 ml), 1 tbsp sugar, 1 drop of vanilla, Ice cubes to half-fill the big bag, 6 tbsp table salt, 1 dish towel, 2 spoons, 1 roll masking tape

  1. Pour the cream into the small bag. She adds the sugar and a drop of vanilla, and smells it first.
  2. Press the bag flat on the table to push the air out, seal it and tape along the seal. Trapped air splits it later.
  3. Open the cold bag, bury the small bag in the ice and salt, and seal it again.
  4. Wrap the dish towel round the parcel and shake. Sing something with a long chorus, hand it over, take it back when her arms go.
  5. At five minutes she presses a finger on the small bag through the towel. It sets at the edges before the middle.
  6. At ten, lift it out, wipe the salt off with the towel, open it and eat out of the bag with the two spoons.

💡Her arms give out long before the ten minutes do. Count the swaps out loud as you pass it back and forth.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Ice Cube Race on the Step

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take four cubes out to the front step on a plate at half past ten, after three hours of July sun on the paving. Two go on the hot slab, two in the shade of the wall. The hot pair is water before you finish talking about it. Put the back of your hand on each slab, then let her put hers on both, and give her one second of a bare foot on the sunny one only if you could hold your own hand there.

Keeping One Cube Till Dinner

Five ice cubes go into five wrappings at one o'clock, and one has to last until dinner.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 9 items

You need: 5 ice cubes the same size, 5 saucers, 1 dish towel, Kitchen foil, Newspaper or shredded paper, 1 shoebox with a lid, 1 small bowl of water, Masking tape and 1 marker, A clock or a phone timer

  1. Tear five strips of tape, number them 1 to 5 with the marker, and she sticks one on each saucer.
  2. Cube 1 sits bare. Cube 2 goes in the folded dish towel, cube 3 in foil, cube 4 buried in shredded newspaper inside the lidded shoebox, cube 5 into the bowl of water. Each stands on its numbered saucer.
  3. Line them up out of the sun. Ask which wins, write all five numbers on a sixth strip of tape stuck to the wall and circle the one she picks to win.
  4. Set the timer for twenty minutes. Each time it goes she opens all five and you cross the dead ones off the wall strip. Leave the kitchen in between, because the timer is what brings her back.
  5. Around three, tell her where this comes from. Men sawed blocks out of frozen lakes in winter, packed them in straw inside a thick-walled ice house and sold that ice in August.
  6. Whichever cube reaches six o'clock goes in a drink at the table, and she names the winner.

💡The bowl of water goes first and she will argue. Water carries heat into a cube faster than air does.
