Day 197 · For the grown-up Ice Cream Without a Freezer · Friday, July 16
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and carrying things while he walks is his project this month. Put your hands over his round the wrapped parcel for two or three shakes. Outside, stand him barefoot on the shaded slab and keep him on it, because the sunny slab has had three hours of July on it.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He goes to the park on his feet rather than in the stroller. Grass at 13 months is uneven and grabs at his shoes, so he staggers the first few steps and then works it out. Give him one thing to carry the whole way.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Celebration is a legitimate way to teach history.

Azlyn cannot hold "before freezers" as a fact. She can hold an afternoon where she wrapped five ice cubes five different ways and one of them lasted until dinner, and the fact rides along inside the memory. Museum educators lean on the same move: give her the practice, the food, the object in her hand, and the dates arrive years later with somewhere to land. She shook a bag for ten minutes to earn one bowl of ice cream, so she knows something true now about what a cold sweet used to cost. Make the treat, eat it, say who else made it this way.

⚠️

Safety: Ice packed in salt drops well below freezing and burns bare skin faster than plain ice does. The parcel stays inside the dish towel and never rests against her arm. Put the back of your hand on the sunny slab before either of them stands on it. If you cannot hold it there, it comes off bare feet and Kreston stays on the shaded side. Loose cubes and spilled salt come off the floor straight away: Kreston walks at 13 months, and a cube he finds is a choking risk. Mid-July sun off a front step burns in twenty minutes, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

The Hatch in the Big Box

⏱️ 60 min🧰 10 items

You need: 1 large cardboard box, tall enough to stand behind, 1 craft knife or heavy scissors (adult only), 1 roll masking tape, 1 permanent marker, 10 sheets of paper, Newspaper for the scoops, 1 flattened box for the menu board, The six-flavor menu sheet from 8:00, Crayons, Cardboard circles cut as coins, palm-sized

  1. Stand her behind the box and mark the hatch with tape at her chest height, wide enough for a tray. Cut it with her standing back, and say why.
  2. Roll the ten sheets into cones. She rolls, you tape the seam, and the wonky ones stay in the pile.
  3. Scrunch newspaper into balls, two scoops a cone. She will make forty of them.
  4. Lay the flattened box down for the menu board and tape this morning's menu sheet to the middle of it. She copies the scoops bigger around the edge in crayon.
  5. Cut the cardboard coins palm-sized, so nothing small reaches the floor. She draws a number on each.
  6. Prop the board against the box, stand behind the hatch and buy something off her. Pay with a coin, wait for change.

💡Cut the hatch narrow. A wide one turns the box into a doorway she walks through.

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take the chalk to the sidewalk outside the front door and let her write the shop's name across it, the flavors underneath and prices she invents. Third week of July, so work in whatever shade the house throws. Anyone walking past gets the menu read at them.

The Jobs She Hands Out

The shop opens at one o'clock with staff, and the rule is that you take the job she gives you.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 8 items

You need: The box shop and the menu board, The paper cones and scoops, The cardboard coins, 1 tray, 1 dish towel as an apron, 1 bell, or a saucepan lid and a spoon, Crayons and 1 marker, A real snack to serve at 3:30

  1. Tuck the dish towel into her waistband as an apron. She rings the bell, or bangs the lid with the spoon, and the shop is open.
  2. She hands out jobs: who scoops, who pays, who carries the tray. Take yours without negotiating.
  3. Everybody lines up with coins and orders off the board. She serves two paper scoops a cone, takes the money and hands back nonsense change. Let it be nonsense.
  4. Swap over. She becomes the customer, you run a bad shop and get her order wrong.
  5. Sit her down with the crayons and the marker to draw each person doing their job on the side of the box. Write the names where she says.
  6. At half past three the real snack goes through the hatch on the tray, and the shop does a round with real food in it.
  7. Leave it standing. She is behind that counter again at quarter past four with nobody watching.

💡She will hand you the dull job on purpose. Line up, complain about the wait, order two scoops of something she invented.

Day 198 · For the grown-up The Ice Cream Shop · Saturday, July 17
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and a chalk stub goes straight to his mouth, so keep it in your own hand with his fingers over yours and let him scrub it on the paving between Azlyn's letters. Keep him on the house side of the path, hat on, and put the back of your hand on the paving before he sits down on it.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

The fish tanks are the whole trip for him at 13 months. Hold him at glass height and stay there while he watches. In the garden center let him walk a wide aisle holding one finger. He stops at every low shelf, and the herbs are worth a touch.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Children describe parents by what they do, not who they are.

Ask a three-year-old about her mother and you get she makes the toast and she does my hair. Azlyn built you out of actions, because actions are the part she can see, and the shop lets her hand them back out. Watch which job she gives you. The person she puts on the register is the one she has filed as the one who sorts things out, and the drawing on the side of the box will tell you the same. Her picture of you is a list of what you do all day, worth knowing on days when that list feels invisible.

⚠️

Safety: The craft knife cuts the hatch and goes back out of reach between cuts, not onto the arm of the sofa. Check inside the box for staples before either child gets near it. Kreston climbs at 13 months, so weight the box down or lay it flat whenever he is loose and you are not beside him. The chalk menu goes on an open sidewalk in the third week of July, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

The Pudding Joseph Remembers

You need: 1 sheet of paper · 1 pen · everybody who is in the house.

  1. Ask Joseph what he ate on hot days when he was small. Let him take his time over the detail, because the detail is the part she repeats later.
  2. She asks everyone else the same question in her own words.
  3. Write the answers down with a name beside each. That list sits on the table until 9:15.

The Tallest Glass in the House

⏱️ 60 min🧰 10 items

You need: 1 tub of ice cream, or Friday's, 4 tall plastic beakers and 4 long spoons, 2 bananas, Canned or fresh fruit, A handful of cookies and 1 bag to crush them in, Jam, loosened with a spoon of hot water, Chocolate sauce, or cocoa and sugar, 1 spoon, 1 index card or cut cereal-box card, and 1 pen, A phone for the photo

  1. Stand the four beakers in a row. Everybody names one layer and she goes round asking. Write each name and layer on the card in order.
  2. She breaks the bananas up with her hands. No knife, and the pieces will be huge.
  3. Cookies into the bag, and she crushes them with her fist against the table.
  4. Loosen the jam with a spoon of hot water yourself and leave it to cool. Cocoa stirred into sugar with a splash of hot water makes the chocolate sauce if there is none in.
  5. Build all four in the order on the card, a scoop of ice cream under each new layer and the canned fruit where the card says. Her hands, your steadying.
  6. Photograph the card next to the beakers before anyone eats, then hand out the long spoons.

💡Her running order is final. Three layers of jam and no fruit is a recipe, and it goes on the card.

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Walk to whatever fruit is ripe within stroller distance in the third week of July. Raspberries on somebody's fence, mulberries down under the tree, the first blackberries if the summer has run warm. She picks into a lidded tub and carries more than she eats, because none of it gets eaten until it is washed at home, and the rest goes in the freezer for tomorrow's pots.

The Tin by the Cookbooks

Clear the table after lunch and fill in four cards, then put them in a tin that stays in this kitchen for years.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: 8–10 index cards or cut cereal-box card, Pens and crayons, 1 cookie tin or shoebox, Masking tape for the label, Old photos, if any are to hand, A phone to photograph each card

  1. One card in front of her at a time. She answers out loud and you write it down.
  2. Card one: what Joseph ate on hot days when he was small, from this morning. Card two: what gets made in this house at birthdays.
  3. Card three: what Brooklyn's family ate that nobody makes now. Card four: the food she wants to be hers, the one people will say is her thing.
  4. She draws on the back of each. Her drawing is the part she will recognize in ten years.
  5. This morning's recipe card joins the pile.
  6. Spread out any old photos to hand. She names who is in them and dictates a line about each onto a card.
  7. Tape a label on the tin and write what she calls it. Photograph every card, then the tin goes on the shelf with the cookbooks.

💡Write what she says, mistakes and all. A card reading strawbrees is worth ten tidy ones.

Day 199 · For the grown-up The Sundae with Everybody In It · Sunday, July 18
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and posts what he picks straight into his mouth, so his share waits until the tub has been through the sink at home. Raspberries and mulberries are soft enough then, squashed between your fingers first. Give him his own empty tub to carry and expect it upended at least once. He wants the walk on his feet, so plan on carrying him home.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Take him on the hunt on foot and let him set the pace, which at 13 months is twenty yards in ten minutes with a stop at every drain. Give him the tub to carry. He picks up whatever is under his feet and hands it to Azlyn.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Food is the most durable carrier of family memory.

Ask an adult what their grandmother's kitchen smelled like and the answer comes back fast. Smell runs straight to the memory and emotion centers of the brain and taste rides along with it, so a food memory arrives whole and lands before any of the words do. Azlyn will lose almost all of this year to the ordinary forgetting of being three. She keeps the sundae with everybody's layer in it, on the condition that you make it again, because repetition turns one afternoon into a tradition. The tin covers your memory as well as hers: the recipes you are certain you could never forget are the first to go.

⚠️

Safety: No nuts, no whole grapes and no hard sprinkles anywhere near Kreston at 13 months. His fruit is mashed and his portion is soft. Only pick what you can name. Anything you are not certain of stays on the bush, and nothing goes in Kreston's mouth unwashed. Jam loosened with hot water scalds, so it cools before she touches it. Plastic beakers rather than glass, and nothing sweet left at his height. A picking walk at eleven has no shade in it, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

Four Pots, Four Names

⏱️ 60 min🧰 7 items

You need: 2 cups plain yogurt (500 g), or 1 tub of vanilla ice cream, softened, 4 small pots or cups with lids, Mix-ins from the cabinet: jam, crushed cookie, cocoa, banana, canned peaches, sprinkles, Sunday's frozen berries, 1 fork and 1 spoon, Paper towels, Masking tape and 1 marker, A cleared freezer shelf

  1. Split the yogurt between the four pots with the spoon. She scrapes, and the four will not come out even.
  2. Line the mix-ins along the table and read the fridge list out. One pot per name.
  3. For each pot she picks what that person would want and says why out loud. Take the reason as it comes, including because he is loud.
  4. She mashes each pot with the fork, one at a time, and the fork gets wiped in between or all four taste the same.
  5. Tape a label on every lid: the name, and her reason underneath in her words.
  6. Lids on and onto the cleared shelf, front row where she can see them. They come out at one o'clock, firm at the edge and soft in the middle.

💡Veto nothing. Cocoa with canned peaches is a decision she made about a person, and she is watching whether her reasons count.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Fishing the Ice Out of the Paddling Pool

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Set the pool up in the shade with three inches of water and tip a tray of ice cubes in. She goes in barefoot and fishes them out by hand, counting them into a cup on the grass, and the game ends when the last one is caught or melted. The pool goes over the flowerbed after.

Which One Is Yours

The pots come out at one o'clock and nobody is told which is theirs. Everybody tastes with their eyes shut and guesses.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: The four frozen pots, Teaspoons for everyone, 1 dish towel for the eyes-shut turns, 1 pitcher of water and paper towels, 4 sheets of paper for cones, Crayons, masking tape and 1 marker

  1. Bring the pots out and turn the lids face down so nobody reads a label early.
  2. Everyone takes a turn with the dish towel over their eyes and a clean teaspoon, tasting all four.
  3. A mouthful of water from the pitcher between tastes, paper towels for the chins.
  4. Each person guesses which pot was made for them. She keeps score on her fingers and gets the count wrong.
  5. Read the labels out. The reason is the part she wants heard, so let her say her own words back with you.
  6. She rolls the four sheets into cones and tapes the seams. You write the flavor name and her reason inside each with the marker, and she covers the outside in crayon.
  7. One cone handed to each person, and whatever is left of the pots goes back in the freezer.

💡Everybody guesses wrong and that is the good bit. Hearing I thought that one was mine tells her the flavors carry something.

Day 200 · For the grown-up A Flavor Named After You · Monday, July 19
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and the pool floor is the hardest surface he has stood on, slick and shifting under him. He drops to sitting inside a minute and slaps the water flat-handed for a long time after that. Sit in with him and float a bath toy where his hands are. He watches Azlyn chase the cubes with the bath toy in his own hands, and the cubes stay on her side of the pool.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

At 13 months he climbs anything with a lip on it, so the toddler frame steps are his whole afternoon. Let him go up, stay a hand's width behind, and count the tries. He goes down the short toddler slide on his own, sitting up and feet first, with you standing at the bottom, and he wants it again the second he lands, pointing rather than crying, which is new.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Admiration is how children choose which traits to grow.

Azlyn is watching the three of you and deciding which bits to keep. She made a pot for each of you this morning out of one noticed thing, and the noticing came first. Children build themselves out of the adults nearest to them, and the traits they copy are the ones they have heard named out loud and approved. Say what you admire in front of her and name the person: Daddy fixes things nobody asks him to fix. She files it. The fridge list records what she has picked up already, and it is worth reading twice before it comes down.

⚠️

Safety: Standing water is the day's hazard. A 13-month-old who walks can drown in the few inches of a paddling pool, in silence and in seconds, so Kreston stays within arm's reach the whole time and the pool gets tipped out the moment you go indoors. The ice stays in Azlyn's half, counted out and counted back in, because a cube in his fist goes to his mouth. Nobody rides a slide with him on a lap, at any age: his shoe catches on the bed, the leg twists, and your weight finishes the break. He goes down the short toddler slide alone, with an adult at the bottom. The pool goes up in the open at half past ten, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

The Three Sounds the Van Makes

You need: 1 metal spoon · 1 saucepan lid · her voice.

  1. Ask what an ice cream van sounds like. Get three sounds out of her: the chime, the engine idling, the hatch sliding open.
  2. She makes each one with her mouth and you copy her, wrong enough that she corrects you.
  3. Settle the chime: three hits of the spoon on the lid, the same three every time. That is the signal for the rest of the day.

The Van That Comes Down Our Street

⏱️ 60 min🧰 8 items

You need: The stroller, or 1 laundry basket, 1 flattened cardboard box for the sign, 1 marker and masking tape, 1 bell, or the metal spoon and saucepan lid, 8 paper cups, The paper scoops from Saturday, or fresh newspaper, Chalk for the stops, 1 tray

  1. Tape the flattened box to the front of the stroller or the side of the basket. She says what the sign says and you write it big.
  2. Load the van: eight paper cups, the paper scoops, the tray laid across the top.
  3. Chalk three stops on the floor if it is tile or vinyl, tape three crosses if it is carpet. She chooses where they go and one of them will be daft.
  4. She pushes, you follow, and the chime rings the whole way. At each stop everybody stops dead and she serves whoever is standing there.
  5. The rule for the round: moving while the chime rings, still when it stops. Vary how long you leave the silence.
  6. Swap over. You push and she rings, which is the harder job, because the person holding the chime decides when everybody else moves.

💡Stopping dead is the part she cannot do and wants to practice. Give her the bell for the last ten minutes and let her catch you moving.

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take the round out to the sidewalk. Chalk three stops along the path: one at the gate, one further than she expects, one at the corner. Then walk the loop with the bell going. Twenty past ten in late July is warm enough that the asphalt smells of it. Serve a cup of water at every stop and let her ring at the neighbor's gate.

Passing the Cone on the Beat

Everybody sits down for this one. One paper cone goes round a circle on a beat she controls by the end of it.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 5 items

You need: 1 paper cone, or 1 paper cup, 1 bell, or the spoon and saucepan lid, A phone with music on it, 4 cushions in a circle, 1 dish towel for the eyes-shut rounds

  1. Cushions in a circle on the floor, everyone sitting close enough to pass without leaning.
  2. Tap the lid at walking pace. The cone moves one person per tap and nobody runs ahead of the beat.
  3. Speed it up until it falls apart, then slow it down to something almost too slow to sit through. She calls fast or slow.
  4. Music on the phone instead of the beat. The music stops and whoever holds the cone names a flavor, and no flavor twice.
  5. Eyes-shut round. Dish towel over her eyes, and she passes and receives by feel while everyone stays quiet.
  6. Hand her the bell. She sets the tempo and the whole circle moves to her hand, which she will test to destruction.
  7. Last round: say the name of the person you are passing to.

💡Nobody goes out and nobody wins. The cone stopping on her is the pleasure, and it evaporates the moment there is a loser in the circle.

Day 201 · For the grown-up The Ice Cream Van · Tuesday, July 20
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and walks the sidewalk round on his own feet, one hand on the rim of the van and one on your finger. He stops at every chalked stop and every gate, so let the round run at his pace. Hat on, and he stays on the house side of you the whole loop.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He is in the water too. At 13 months he walks the shallow end holding both your hands and pushes against the drag, which is hard work and he will do it until he is cold. Twenty-five minutes is plenty. Get him out while he is still enjoying it and feed him inside the half hour.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Moving in time with someone builds connection, measurably.

Rocking a baby in time with your own breathing, clapping a rhythm, walking in step: children who move in synchrony with an adult go on to help that adult more and share with them more, and the effect shows up in four-year-olds in the lab within minutes of a shared beat. Azlyn passing a cone round a circle on your tap is doing something older than any of the words in it. She is matching her timing to everybody else in the circle and feeling what that is like. On a day when she has been contrary since breakfast, a shared rhythm resets more than a conversation will.

⚠️

Safety: An adult keeps a hand on the stroller out on the sidewalk, whoever is doing the pushing, and the round stays this side of the curb. At the pool Kreston is within arm's reach every second he is in the water, and armbands are not a substitute for your hands. Kreston walks the round on his own feet and goes faster than he can stop, so he stays on the house side of you the whole loop with one hand on the van and one on your finger. The sidewalk round runs in open sun, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

  1. Lay a sheet flat. Write the name across the top with the marker and the reason underneath in her words.
  2. She turns it over and draws a scoop on the back in that person's color, felt pens or crayons as she likes.

The Sundae She Doesn't Eat

One bowl gets made this afternoon for somebody who is out of the house, and it waits in the freezer with a place set at the table.

You need: 1 lidded pot or bowl, Ice cream, or a leftover pot from Monday, 1 topping she chooses for that person, 1 name card, 1 pen and crayons, 1 spoon, a scrap of paper and masking tape for the flag, Freezer space at the front of a shelf

👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and a mail slot flap is the best posting slot he has met. Hold the flap open and let him push the second cone through. He will let go too early and want it back, so keep one hand on it. Walking with something in his fist and giving it up on purpose are two different jobs, and he is halfway through the second.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Take him to the board-book corner and put him down. At 13 months he walks the shelves with one hand out, pulling books off as he goes, and putting them back is your job rather than his. Let Azlyn choose one for him and carry it to the desk. He will hold it the whole way home.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Gratitude needs a target before it needs a feeling.

Telling a three-year-old to be grateful gets you a flat thank you aimed at nobody. Azlyn spent this morning naming eight people and what each of them did, which is the part that does the work. Gratitude research keeps landing in the same place: the benefit lands when a person can say who helped, what they did and what it cost them. She cannot hold all three yet, so she practices the first two with a cone in her hand and a name written inside it. Ask her who did something today at dinner and you get a real answer, which is the habit underneath the feeling.

⚠️

Safety: The scissors are the only hazard on the table and they cut paper faster than anything she has used. They come out for the trim and go back on a high shelf between cones, never left down while Kreston is walking the room. The walk to the two doors runs at half past ten in late July, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you.

Sweet Enough to Freeze

You need: the juice · 2 cups · 1 tsp sugar · half a lemon · 1 spoon.

  1. Pour a little juice into each cup, the same amount in both, and leave the other 1 2/3 cups for 9:15.
  2. Stir the teaspoon of sugar and a squeeze of lemon into the second cup until the grains are gone.
  3. She tastes both and calls which is sweeter. Tell her sweet water freezes soft enough to scrape and plain water freezes into a brick, and the tray goes in at 9:15.

The Tray That Gets Scraped

⏱️ 60 min🧰 8 items

You need: 1 shallow metal or plastic tray, 1 2/3 cups juice or blitzed watermelon (400 ml), 2 tbsp sugar, Half a lemon, 1 fork, 1 length of string and 8 clothespins, Masking tape and 1 marker, A cleared flat freezer shelf

  1. Stir the sugar and the juice of the half lemon into the 1 2/3 cups until no grains are left on the bottom. She stirs, you check.
  2. Pour it into the tray, a finger deep and no deeper, and she carries it flat to the cleared shelf.
  3. Tape one end of the string to the fridge and the other to a cupboard handle, pulled taut at her height. She clips all eight pegs along it.
  4. Write READY on a strip of tape and stick it past the last peg, so the end of the line is a place.
  5. Every half hour from half past nine, open the freezer and drag the fork across the tray, breaking the frozen edges into the middle. She takes one peg off each time.
  6. Two pegs are still on the line at lunch. Leave them.

💡Scrape, do not stir. Dragging the fork across the top makes crystals; stirring makes slush that sets solid.

👶 Infant integration morning

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Waiting is easier when it's visible and shrinking.

Azlyn has no working sense of half an hour. Eight pegs on a string give her one, because the line gets shorter in front of her and she is the one taking them off. Children wait longer and complain less when the wait is represented by something they can see and act on, which is why sticker charts work and soon does not. The wait also gets easier when she has a job inside it, and the fork scrape is that job. Use the same trick on car journeys and doctors' waiting rooms: something countable, going down, in her hands.

⚠️

Safety: Hard chunks of ice are a choking hazard for Kreston at 13 months, so his portion is scraped fine and slushy and handed to him sitting down. Pick the seeds out of his watermelon wedge before he gets it, because a seed is throat-sized at this age, and the spitting target goes on a tray so the seeds land somewhere you can lift away rather than on the path he sits on. A metal tray out of the freezer sticks to wet hands, so it comes out on a dish towel. Keep the freezer door shut between scrapes, because he climbs and pulls now, and take the string down the moment the last peg comes off. The back step catches the sun all morning: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

Day 204
One Fish, Three Ways
The Big Book of Little Days · July · Week 29Day 203 · for the grown-up
July · Week 30

Under the Sea 🌊

July 23 – July 29, 2027 · Days 204–210

Azlyn builds a sea this week and it stays up. You tape a blue sheet down one wall on Friday and she hangs three fish in it at three depths, and on Saturday the staircase becomes the water column, bright at the top and black at the bottom. By Monday a whale the size of a door hangs beside the fish, and Tuesday adds a jellyfish in a doorway the grown-ups and Azlyn duck through. One question runs underneath all the making: what floats, what sinks, and what changes the answer. She meets it in a squeezed bottle on Sunday morning, in three tubs loaded pebble by pebble after lunch, and again on Thursday with an egg and six spoonfuls of salt.

No holiday lands in this week. Wednesday carries something else, because six months of the book are behind you and the day is built to mark them. Azlyn answers four questions into a bottle that gets taped shut until New Year's Eve, lays January to June along the wall in six sheets and her own words, and finishes at the door frame with a pencil mark beside January's. The other thing shaping these seven days is late July heat. Shade by eleven, water every half hour, and Thursday afternoon spent flat on cushions in the coolest room in the house with a blue flashlight.

🧒 What Azlyn will learn
  • One fish, three techniques. Torn paper, a fork dipped in paint and a hand traced round, all making the same animal, and she starts choosing the method to suit the picture in her head.
  • Comparing length without numbers. A string cut to her own height goes round the house, then five more cut to a seahorse, an octopus, a dolphin, a shark and a blue whale.
  • Floating and sinking as one idea. A sauce packet in a squeezed bottle, three tubs loaded until the water comes over the rim, and an egg that rides high in salty water.
  • Painting from the shoulder. A wide brush on the floor and a six-foot wave, which is the arm work that has to happen before she can steer a pencil.
  • Forty days and six months of her own change. June's five ticked test cards beside what she can do today, her words written down as she says them, and two pencil marks on a door frame with a gap between them.
👶 KRESTON THIS WEEK

Kreston is 13 months this week. He walks, climbs onto anything with a rim or a step, and carries things about while he moves. Water and cut string are both at his height this week, so the bowls go out and the string goes up the moment you stop watching him.

The Big Book of Little Days · JulyWeek 30 · opener →
🌍 Around the world Week 30 · read it on Day 204

Pacific Wayfinding 🌊

Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of miles of open Pacific with no compass and no chart. They read the swell under the hull, the stars rising along the horizon, the green light a lagoon throws onto cloud, and the flight lines of birds heading home at dusk. Hawaiian crews still sail the double canoe Hōkūleʻa that way.

✨
Try it

The Blue Paper Hunt

The Same Fish Three Times

⏱️ 60 min🧰 7 items

You need: Blue and green paper scraps: junk mail, wrapping paper, magazines, 1 glue stick, or flour and water paste in a saucer, 3 sheets of thick paper, Washable poster paint, blue and white, 1 saucer and 1 fork, 1 pencil and 1 marker, 1 wet washcloth

  1. Sheet one is the torn fish. She tears a body, a tail and a fin from the scraps and sticks them flat with the glue stick or the paste.
  2. Sheet two is the printed fish. Draw the outline in pencil, then blue paint and a blob of white into the saucer, half mixed.
  3. Show her the back of the fork once: press, lift, move along. She fills the outline with rows of scales.
  4. Wipe her hands with the wet washcloth before sheet three.
  5. Sheet three is the hand fish. Draw round her flat hand with the pencil, thumb out for the fin, go over the line with the marker and let her put the eye in.
  6. Stand all three against the wall and ask which one goes in the middle this afternoon.

💡She will want the fork fish to look like the torn one. Say out loud that this is one fish made three ways: torn, printed, drawn.

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Hats on and out before the sidewalk gets hot. Count every blue thing between your door and the end of the street: a recycling bin, a parked car, a road sign, a front door. Ask her for the palest blue she can find, then the darkest. Pale at the top, dark at the bottom goes up on the wall at 1:00.

The Ocean Down One Wall

One wall of the house goes under water for the rest of the week. Pick the wall she walks past most, because Monday's whale goes on it too, and Tuesday's jellyfish hangs in a doorway beside it.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 7 items

You need: 1 blue sheet, blue plastic tablecloth or 2 blue trash bags, 1 roll masking tape, String, 6 feet, The three fish from this morning, Scissors (adult only), Scrap paper and crayons for more creatures, 1 flashlight

  1. Tape the sheet flat to the wall, top edge as high as you can reach and the bottom on the baseboard.
  2. Cut three lengths of string, long, middling and short. She holds, you cut.
  3. Tape a string to the back of each fish. Palest at the top, darkest at the bottom. She decides where the third one belongs.
  4. Scrap paper and crayons on the floor. She draws more creatures, you cut them out, and every one gets a depth before it goes up.
  5. Shut the curtains, turn the big light off and give her the flashlight. The bottom of the wall is the part the sun never reaches.
  6. Lie on the floor together with your feet to the baseboard and look up through the whole thing.

💡Let her keep the flashlight and light one creature at a time from the floor, and say nothing.

Day 204 · For the grown-up One Fish, Three Ways · Friday, July 23
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and carries things while he walks, so give him a job with a destination. One torn blue scrap, handed over, carried across the room, posted into the tray. On the street let him walk a stretch of it holding your finger.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He is 13 months and climbing, so the low end of the wall belongs to him. Tape one spare paper fish at his eye level and expect it pulled off within the hour. Tape it back. Lift him up to pat the palest fish at the top before you set him down.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Three techniques for one outcome teaches technique as a concept.

One fish three ways hands Azlyn something a single fish cannot. She holds the idea of the fish steady while the method underneath it keeps changing, and that split, subject on one side and technique on the other, is where choosing a tool for a job begins. Ask a three-year-old to draw a fish and you get the fish she can already draw. Give her a fork and the same fish arrives through a different door. Children who work across materials carry skills between them, and the carrying shows up later as range. By four she will pick the material to suit the picture in her head.

⚠️

Safety: The scissors are adult-only and go back out of reach between cuts. Kreston is 13 months and walks over to whatever you are doing, so the glue stick, the torn paper and the string go up on the table the moment you stop watching him. Trim the hanging string ends short and leave no loop at his height. Washable non-toxic paint only. The street walk runs in open sun before eleven, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

The String That Is Azlyn Long

You need: 1 ball of string · scissors (adult only) · masking tape · 1 marker.

  1. She lies flat on the floor. Run string from her heels to the top of her head and cut it there.
  2. Wrap a tab of masking tape round one end and write AZLYN on it with the marker.
  3. Carry it round the house. The bath, the sofa, the front door, the car. Longer than Azlyn, shorter than Azlyn. That is the only measuring she does today.

The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

A String for Every Creature

⏱️ 60 min🧰 7 items

You need: 1 ball of string, Scissors (adult only), 1 tape measure, Masking tape, 1 marker, Sticky labels or scrap paper, 6 clothespins to hold the ends

  1. Write five names on the labels with the marker: seahorse, octopus, dolphin, great white shark, blue whale.
  2. Measure with the tape measure and cut while she holds the far end. Seahorse 6 inches. Octopus 3 feet. Dolphin 8 feet. Great white shark 16 feet.
  3. Clip the right label to each length and keep the spare peg for the whale.
  4. The blue whale runs to 80 feet and will not fit in the house. Unroll that much, peg its label on and coil it by the door.
  5. Lay the four indoor lengths against real things: the seahorse against her hand, the octopus against the bath, the shark taped flat down the hallway.
  6. Line them up shortest to longest and ask which is longer, the dolphin or the shark, with both in front of her.

💡Skip numbers when she asks how big. Say longer than the sofa and shorter than you. Sixteen feet means nothing to her yet. The sofa means a great deal.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Chalking the Whale Down the Path

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take the whale string and the chalk. Find the longest run of sidewalk near you with no driveways across it, peg one end at your gate, walk backwards with the ball until the string runs out, and chalk a fat line at each end. Eighty feet of sidewalk, one animal. She will run it end to end six times. She stops on the chalk at the edge of any driveway that cuts the run, looks both ways, and waits for you before she crosses.

Down the Stairs to the Bottom of the Sea

The staircase is the water column until bedtime, bright at the top and black at the bottom.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: Paper, 10 sheets, Crayons, Masking tape, 1 flashlight, The string lengths from this morning, 1 cushion for the bottom step

  1. Sit on the top step with the paper and crayons. The top stair is the surface: bright blue, warm, full of light.
  2. Work downward one stair at a time. Each sheet gets a darker sky than the one above, and the last three get black and nothing else.
  3. She draws one creature per sheet. Seahorse near the top, dolphin lower, shark lower again, and something with its own light at the bottom.
  4. Tape each drawing to the riser of its stair as she finishes it.
  5. Lay the octopus and dolphin strings flat along the treads beside their pictures, so the real length runs next to the drawing. Coil both and put them away before the curtains shut.
  6. Shut the curtains at the foot of the stairs, put the cushion on the bottom step and sit down with the light off.
  7. Flashlight on, one creature at a time. Down here the only light is the light an animal brings with it.

💡Let her hold the flashlight and choose the order. Ten minutes sitting in the dark naming animals is worth more than the drawing was.

Day 205 · For the grown-up How Long Is a Whale · Saturday, July 24
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and walks with a wide, busy gait that eats distance. Set him down at the tail end of the chalked whale and let him make his own way along it beside you. He stops at every drain and gatepost, so allow the whole forty-five minutes for a length Azlyn covers in fifteen seconds.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

At 13 months the stairs are the most interesting object in his life and he heads for them the moment the gate opens. Sit him on your lap on the bottom step for the flashlight part. Give him a spare sheet of paper and a crayon on the hall floor.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Measuring by comparison comes before measuring by number.

A string that is Azlyn long does a job a ruler cannot do for another three years. She cannot hold a shark and a dolphin side by side, so she compares each one against a third thing she can carry around, and the third thing settles it. Mathematicians call the finished version transitivity: this beats that, that beats the sofa, so the ranking follows without laying all three together. Working it out in her head comes some years after three. Today she runs the physical version on the hallway floor, one string at a time against one object, and the later reasoning grows out of that groundwork. Give her the comparing first and the numbers have somewhere to sit.

⚠️

Safety: Cut string is today's hazard. A loop at his height is a strangulation risk, so nothing goes over the banister and every length is coiled and out of the stairwell before the flashlight part starts. Never leave Kreston alone in a room with one, and keep the stair gate shut while the drawings go up. Azlyn stops on the chalk at the edge of any driveway the route has to cross and looks both ways first, you keep a hand on Kreston past every one, and you lift the whale string off the sidewalk while anybody walks through. Eighty feet of open sidewalk holds no shade: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you.

Water Above the Rim

You need: 1 clear 2-liter bottle with its cap · 1 pitcher · 1 bowl · 1 old towel.

  1. Towel on the table, bowl on the towel, bottle in the bowl. She pours from the pitcher and the bowl catches what misses.
  2. Fill it to the neck, then past it, until the water bulges above the rim. She will spill it, and that is what the bowl is for.
  3. Cap on, tip it over and hunt for the bubble at the top. No bubble is the target, and she will fill it three times to get there.

The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

The Diver in the Bottle

⏱️ 60 min🧰 6 items

You need: 1 clear 2-liter plastic bottle with its cap, 1 ketchup or soy sauce packet (substitute: a pen cap with a small blob of poster putty or modeling clay on the clip), Water, 1 pitcher, 1 bowl to catch the spills, 1 old towel

  1. Half fill the bottle from the pitcher and drop the packet in. It wants to float with one corner breaking the surface. A packet that sinks straight down is the wrong one.
  2. Top the bottle up over the bowl until the water stands proud of the rim, then screw the cap down hard.
  3. Squeeze the sides with both hands. The diver sinks. Let go and it rises. Do it once, then hand her the bottle.
  4. Stand back. She will run it forty times without help, and the towel is there because she hugs the bottle to her chest.
  5. Ask her to make it stop halfway, then to tell you what she is doing to it.

💡Nothing happening means the bottle is not full to the brim. Air in the neck soaks up the squeeze, so top it up over the bowl and try again.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The River Down the Driveway

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

A pitcher of water tipped out at the top of the drive makes a river, and hot July paving drinks it in four minutes. Chalk two lanes down the slope and race a pour down each, one in your hand and one in hers, calling which reaches the bottom first. Then watch a wet lane shrink from both ends and chalk a mark where the water gave up.

How Many Pebbles Until It Goes Under

Three empty tubs out of the recycling, pebbles counted in one at a time, and a number chalked under each tub at the moment it gives up.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: 3 plastic tubs in three sizes: a yogurt pot, a margarine tub, an ice cream tub, 1 dishpan or the paddling pool, A bag of pebbles, or a jar of coins, Chalk, 1 pitcher, 2 towels

  1. Stand the bowl in the shade and fill it from the pitcher. One towel down beside it.
  2. Line the three tubs up on the paving smallest to biggest and let her hold each one empty on the flat of her hand.
  3. Chalk a big 1, 2 and 3 under them and ask which tub takes the most pebbles before anything touches the water.
  4. Float tub one and load pebbles in one at a time, counting out loud, until the water comes over the rim. Chalk that number under the 1.
  5. Ask her for tub two's number before it goes anywhere near the water. Run two, then three, the same way, one pebble at a time, and chalk each number under its tub.
  6. Stand back with her and read all three off the paving in a row. Three sizes, one job, and the numbers say what the size did.
  7. Tip the bowl out over the hot paving, dry her hands and feet with the second towel, and count the pebbles back into the bag.

💡Keep the one-at-a-time rule for all three. The idea sits in the single pebble that takes a tub under, and a fistful hides it.

Day 206 · For the grown-up Float, Sink, Squeeze · Sunday, July 25
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months, and hot paving with water running over it is the best five minutes of his morning. Sit him at the top of the slope with the curb a long way below him and let him slap at the water going past. Give him his own cup to fill and spill.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He is 13 months and climbs into anything with a rim, the dishpan included. Give him a fourth tub of his own to carry about and drop. Once the bowl is empty he walks the wet paving barefoot and watches his footprints dry.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Recognizing the same principle in new clothes is real understanding.

Azlyn met floating in a bottle at 9:15 and meets it again in a bowl of water after lunch, and the second meeting is where it sticks. A child who sees one idea in one setting files it as a fact about that object: this packet goes down when you squeeze. Show her the same idea in different clothes and it turns into a rule about the world. Researchers call the move transfer, and it is the hardest part of teaching. One sentence at the bowl helps it along. This is the same as the bottle, isn't it. Then let her tell you how.

⚠️

Safety: Standing water and a 13-month-old who walks. The bowl and the pool get emptied the moment you stop watching, with no exception for a trip indoors, and he stays within arm's reach whenever either holds water. The packet, the pen cap, the pebbles and the coins are all choking-sized and stay in your pocket between turns. The driveway ends at a live road, so run the pours on the top half of the slope, keep the finish a stride short of the curb, and hold his hand from the curb onward with the road on your side of him. Late July puts the sun overhead by eleven: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

  2. Lay them edge to edge into one long strip and weight the corners with the stones so the wind cannot lift them.

Painting the Waves With Both Arms

⏱️ 60 min🧰 7 items

You need: 3–4 large cardboard boxes, cut open flat, Washable poster paint, blue and white, 1 wide house-painting brush, 1 sponge cut in half, 2 shallow trays or old plates, 1 bucket of water and an old towel, Old clothes for both of them

  1. Blue in one tray, white in the other. Old clothes on, and say out loud that the paint is allowed to go everywhere.
  2. Show her one stroke with the house-painting brush and make it enormous: shoulder swinging, arm straight, the line running the length of a board.
  3. She paints wave after wave down the strip. Say bigger rather than neater, and keep saying it.
  4. Half a sponge dipped in white and dragged along the top of each wave makes the foam. The dry half lifts color back off.
  5. Once the boards are covered, rinse the brush in the bucket and let her wash her arms in it before the towel, then tip the water out over the grass.
  6. Drag the boards into full shade to dry and leave them until after lunch.

💡Big arm work goes wrong at a table, where her elbow stays pinned to her ribs. On the floor with a wide brush she paints from the shoulder.

She draws one whale the size of a door, and it takes both of you to get it up the hall.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: The dry painted cardboard, 1 permanent marker, Heavy scissors or a craft knife (adult only), Masking tape, Scrap card for a tail and a fin, String, 3 feet

  1. Pick the best-painted board. Give her the marker and one instruction: a whale that fills the whole thing, corner to corner.
  2. Let the line be hers. She stands over the board and draws from the shoulder, and you leave the outline alone.
  3. Cut it out yourself with the knife or the heavy scissors while she stands back, and say why.
  4. She draws a tail and a fin on the scrap card, you cut those out, and she tapes them on wherever she thinks they belong.
  5. Carry it into the house together, one end each, turning it sideways at the doorway.
  6. Tape one end of the string to the whale's back and the other high on the wall above Friday's blue sheet, so the tail hangs free.
  7. Look at it with her from the far end of the room, from where the sofa is. She has never made anything this big.

💡She will want to add detail once it is up. Give her the marker and let her, because a whale she keeps adding to is one she keeps coming back to.

Day 207 · For the grown-up Painting the Sea · Monday, July 26
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months, and long grass at his height is a wall he has to push through, which is hard, hot work for a new walker. He climbs now, so a low bank or a fallen branch is a better use of his legs. Check him for grass seeds and ticks at home.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Keep him well away from the cutting, then bring him in for the carrying. At 13 months he carries things while he walks and will want a piece of the whale to hold, so hand him an offcut of card that is his.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Big arm movements are still building the hand that will write.

The wide brush and the shoulder swing are groundwork for handwriting. Control develops from the middle of the body outward, so a trunk and a shoulder that can hold steady come before an elbow that can hold steady, which comes before fingers that can steer a pencil. Azlyn painting a six-foot wave is loading the joints a five-year-old needs braced before her fingers can do anything fine. Vertical and floor-level surfaces do this better than a table does, because her arm has to hold its own weight while it works. Every big sweeping hour now buys quiet control at a desk later.

⚠️

Safety: The craft knife is adult-only and goes back out of reach between cuts, on a shelf rather than the arm of a chair. Kreston is 13 months and a walker, so stay within arm's reach of the paint bucket while it stands full, and tip it out over the grass at step 5. A July morning on a paved path needs shade, hats and water within reach. Dark cardboard in full sun gets hot enough to burn bare feet, so keep the boards shaded and move them as the sun comes round. Two stretches outdoors today: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

  1. Lay the five cards out in front of her before anything gets wet. She reads each one back off her own drawing.
  2. Ask which of the five she can do better now. Take the answer and leave it alone, because the pool settles it in an hour.
  3. Water finished, plate cleared, swim things on. She has agreed to the whole morning before she notices.

The Five Tests Again, Forty Days On

⏱️ 60 min🧰 9 items

You need: Paddling pool, or the bath, The five ticked cards from June, 1 timer, 1 whistle, or the shout word instead, 1 teddy, 1 empty capped 2-liter bottle on a short line, 3 towels, Sun cream and a hat, Your phone

  1. Pool in the shade and filled shallow, sun cream on, hat on, towels within reach. Lay the five cards along the edge in June's order and photograph her doing each test with its card in the shot.
  2. The float. She lies back on your hand, ears down, chin up, and the timer runs a minute. In June your whole hand was under her back for it.
  3. The bubbles. Chin on the water, mouth under, hum out past ten if she can, because that is where the forty days show.
  4. The reach. Teddy goes out past her arms. She throws the bottle beyond him and pulls it back so it sweeps him in, feet staying out.
  5. The shout, then the whistle. Her whole name and HELP, loud enough for next door. Then, while she plays, one blow on the whistle: she stops dead and comes to the edge.
  6. Out over the wall of the pool without a hand from you and into the towel. Put the line and the whistle away, and let her carry the five cards back inside.

💡Hold each card up beside what she has done and read it out as a fact. She cannot feel forty days of change from inside; the June card hands it to her.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Naming the Ground With Her Eyes Shut

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

She walked five grounds barefoot in mid-July and named each as she arrived. Today she names them first. Shoes off, your hand on her shoulder, her eyes shut, and stop her a step short of each surface: mown grass, paving, gravel, a doormat, bare soil under a tree. She calls it, then puts a foot down and finds out whether she was right. Put the back of your hand on each surface first, and if you could not hold it there it comes off bare feet.

The Jellyfish in the Doorway

Two paper bowls and a grocery bag turn into a jellyfish that hangs in a doorway the grown-ups and Azlyn walk through all week.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 7 items

You need: 2 paper bowls or paper plates, 1 grocery bag cut into strips, or ribbon, String, 3 feet, Masking tape, 1 marker, 1 pencil to make the holes, Scissors (adult only)

  1. Tape the two bowls rim to rim into a dome. She holds them together while you run the tape round, as messy as it comes out.
  2. She draws the face on with the marker. Jellyfish have no face, and hers is getting one.
  3. Cut the grocery bag into long strips while she sorts them into short ones and long ones.
  4. Tape the strips round the rim one at a time, wherever she points. Twenty is not too many.
  5. Push the pencil through the top of the dome, thread the string through the hole and knot it fat so it cannot pull back out.
  6. Hang it at Azlyn's head height in a doorway you can gate or shut against Kreston. In a doorway he walks through, trim every strip level with the dome rim so nothing hangs where he can grab it.
  7. She walks through it, backs up and walks through it again. Turn the hall light off once the sun drops.

💡Hang it where somebody has to walk through it. Ducking under a jellyfish every time you cross that doorway is the payoff.

Day 208 · For the grown-up Forty Days Stronger · Tuesday, July 27
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and barefoot walking is useful work for him, because bare soles feed his balance better than a shoe does. Take him along the same five surfaces holding one of your hands, and expect him to sit down hard on the gravel. He goes on nothing you could not hold the back of your hand against.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He is 13 months and walks in the shallows now rather than sitting in them, which means he heads for deep water with total confidence and no ability. Keep him inside arm's reach for the whole session with your hands free. Twenty minutes is plenty, and Azlyn can hand him his towel.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Repeating an activity across the year makes growth visible.

Running the same five tests in June and again today gives you something a milestone chart never will: her, against her, forty days apart. Azlyn cannot perceive her own development. She has no memory of being the child who could not hum out a count of ten, so praise about how much she has grown lands as noise, while her own June card held up beside this morning lands as evidence. Do it for yourself as well. The days run together at this age and progress hides inside them, so a repeated test drags it into the open. Keep the cards and run the five again in September.

⚠️

Safety: Water twice today, the pool this morning and the real one at 2:30. Both children stay inside arm's reach at both, close enough to take hold of without a step. While your hand is under her back for the float, Kreston sits in the water beside her or in the shade in front of you, and the paddling pool goes onto its side the second you go indoors. The jellyfish hangs behind a gate or a shut door, because the string and twenty plastic strips sit inside a 13-month-old's reach and a strip he pulls down goes to his mouth. In a doorway he uses, the strips come level with the dome rim. Two rounds of sun: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven, and once more on dry skin before you leave. The scissors stay with you.

Peeling the Label Off

You need: 1 clear plastic bottle with a screw cap · 1 bowl of warm water · 1 old towel.

  1. Stand the bottle in the bowl of warm water while she eats. Warm water loosens the glue and does the hard part for her.
  2. Let her pick the label off in one piece if she can and in forty pieces if she cannot. Thumbnails only, no rush.
  3. Dry it with the towel. Tell her something is going inside it this morning that stays shut until New Year's Eve, then say no more about it.

The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

The Message in the Bottle

⏱️ 60 min🧰 6 items

You need: 1 clear plastic bottle with a screw cap, Paper cut into strips, Crayons and a pen, Ribbon or string, Packing tape, A spoonful of sand or a few small stones

  1. Strips laid out on the table. Ask her four questions and write the answers word for word with the pen: her favorite thing about this summer, who she plays with, what she is good at, what she wants to be doing at Christmas.
  2. Leave her grammar alone. The wrong words are the ones you will want in December.
  3. She fills two more strips with crayon drawings and tells you what each one is. Write the caption underneath.
  4. Write your own strip while she works. Do not read it out, and fold it before it goes in.
  5. Roll every strip and tie it with a scrap of ribbon. She posts them into the bottle one at a time.
  6. Add the spoonful of sand yourself, screw the cap down, run packing tape round the cap and write OPEN NEW YEAR'S EVE across the tape with the pen. Stand it on the shelf beside January's sealed box, where she can see it and not reach it.

💡She will ask to open it tomorrow. Give her the distance in things she knows: after the leaves come off, after the snow, after her birthday.

Walk down to the drain on the corner with a pitcher of water and tip it in. Listen for where it lands. Then give her the plain version: the water in that hole ends up in the river, and the river ends up in the sea she has been building all week. Look at what else has gone down there.

Six Months of Azlyn on the Wall

Six sheets, one for each month gone, and she tells you what she remembers. Some months she will have nothing. Some she will have one sentence that stops you where you stand.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 7 items

You need: 6 sheets of paper, Crayons, Masking tape, 1 pencil, The photos on your phone, The growth chart wall or door frame, The handprint sheets, if they are to hand

  1. Write a month across the top of each sheet, January through June, and lay them out on the floor.
  2. Take one month at a time. Show her three or four photos and ask what she remembers. Write what she says on that month's sheet, in her words.
  3. She draws the thing she named with the crayons. One drawing a month is plenty and a scribble counts.
  4. Tape the six along the wall in a line at her height, so the year reads left to right.
  5. Move to the door frame. Heels flat, back straight, pencil mark, today's date beside it.
  6. Show her January's mark underneath and let her put her fingers in the gap. That gap is the six months on the wall, measured in her.
  7. Lay the handprint sheets under the row and let her fit her hand onto January's.

💡She will remember odd things. A bee, a broken cup, somebody's shoes. Write the odd ones down word for word and let go of the birthday you were angling for.

Day 209 · For the grown-up Halfway Through the Year · Wednesday, July 28
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and posts things through holes with great commitment, which makes a street drain a problem. Keep hold of his hand at the curb and give him something bigger than the gaps, a plastic cup or a stick. Let him drop leaves through the grating and count them going in with him.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He goes on the door frame today too, standing up this time, heels against the wood and your hand flat on his head. At 13 months that is a real measurement. Give him his own sheet of paper and a crayon on the floor under the row of months.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

The halfway point is worth marking for you as much as for her.

Six months of this is a great many mornings, and most of them left no trace you can point at. Azlyn will not remember January. You will, and the row of sheets on the wall is there for you: proof that the hours went into something, on a Wednesday in July when it does not feel that way. Parents underrate their own consistency because the evidence disperses into ordinary days, and photographs, a door frame and a bottle on a shelf gather it back up. Stand and look at the row for a minute before you take it down. You built the six months it records.

⚠️

Safety: The sand, the small stones and the ribbon are all choking-sized, so they stay in your pocket between steps and go away before Kreston is down on the floor. Once the tape is on, the bottle goes straight up on the shelf out of his reach. At the drain, hold his hand from the curb onward and keep the grating on your side of him. The walk to the corner and back is twenty minutes of open sun, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

Stirring Until It Vanishes

You need: 1 clear jar · 1 pitcher of water · table salt · 1 spoon.

  1. Half fill the jar from the pitcher and let her tip a spoonful of salt in. It sits on the bottom in a white heap.
  2. Hand her the spoon. Stirring until the heap disappears takes longer than she expects.
  3. Ask her where the salt went, then get her to dip a fingertip in this weak jar and taste it. Leave the question open until this afternoon.

The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

Making Sea Water

⏱️ 60 min🧰 7 items

You need: 3 clear jars or pint glasses, Table salt, 1 raw egg (a small potato also works), 1 spoon, 1 pitcher of water, 1 dark plate for the sun test, Masking tape and a marker for the labels

  1. Tape a label on each jar and write 0, 1 and 6 with the marker. She fills all three from the pitcher to the same height.
  2. Jar 0 stays plain. One spoonful of salt into jar 1. Six into jar 6, stirred until the water goes clear again.
  3. Lower the egg into jar 0. It sits flat on the bottom. Try jar 1, where it sits on the bottom again. She met this egg and this jar in March, so let her tell you what happens next.
  4. Jar 6. The egg lifts off the bottom and rides at the top with a coin of shell showing, and she will ask you to do it again.
  5. Let her move the egg between the jars as long as she wants.
  6. Pour a splash from jar 6 onto the dark plate and stand it in full sun. Come back at snack time to a white crust of salt.

💡March's jar had no name on it. Today it has one: jar 6 is the sea, jar 0 is the tap, and the crust on the plate is what the sea leaves behind.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Painting the Fence With Water

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

A bucket of water, a wide brush each, and the fence in the shade. She paints and the water vanishes behind her, which on a hot morning takes four minutes. Race the drying: a big letter A at one end, then a run back to see whether it survived.

The Deep, Dark, Cold Room

The coolest room in the house becomes the bottom of the sea for the afternoon.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 9 items

You need: The fish, the whale and the jellyfish from this week, 1 flashlight, 1 blue grocery bag or blue cellophane, and an elastic band, 1 sheet, 2 dining chairs, 2 heavy books or bags to weight the chair legs, A fan, if you have one, Cold drinks and a cold wet washcloth each, Cushions

  1. Shut the curtains and turn the lights off. Bring the fish, the whale and the jellyfish in, hang the jellyfish high and tape the fish and the whale flat to the walls.
  2. Drape the sheet over the two chair backs for a low roof in one corner, weight the legs with the books and push the cushions underneath.
  3. Stretch the blue grocery bag over the head of the flashlight and hold it with the elastic band. Everything the beam lands on goes blue.
  4. Set the fan on the floor pointing at the cushions and let her feel the moving air with her eyes shut.
  5. Cold drinks, and a washcloth each over the back of the neck.
  6. Lie under the sheet with the blue flashlight and pick out one creature at a time. She names each and tells you how deep it lives.
  7. Stay down there until half two. Everything between now and then happens on those cushions.

💡A hot three-year-old will fight a rest and take a game, and this one has her flat on her back inside ten minutes.

Day 210 · For the grown-up Sea Water and Shade · Thursday, July 29
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and this is the easiest win of his day: one paintbrush, one shallow tub of water, one fence. He carries the brush about and paints the ground, the wall and himself. Keep his hat on and offer him water every twenty minutes.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

At 13 months he climbs onto anything, so weight the chairs holding the sheet and expect him to pull it down at least once. Let him have his own cold washcloth to chew and carry, and offer him a drink every half hour.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Heat makes children behave badly, and it isn't a discipline problem.

Azlyn heats up faster than you do, for reasons that are all plumbing. She carries more skin per pound of body, so July gets at her from a wider surface. Her sweat glands are all present and still running at a fraction of adult output, which is her main cooling system working at half power. She generates more heat per pound while she moves, and her thirst arrives late, behind the fluid she has already lost. Shade by eleven, water every half hour, and a cold washcloth on the back of the neck are the levers that work on that body.

⚠️

Safety: A fingertip off the weak jar at 8:00 is the point of the activity. Jar 6 is not for tasting, salt water is dangerous to drink, and a 13-month-old will try any of it, so all three jars and the dark plate stay where Kreston cannot reach them and get poured away before the floor picnic. His tub at the fence and Azlyn's bucket are both shallow enough to look harmless and deep enough to drown in, so you stay within arm's reach of him while either one holds water, and you tip both out the moment the brushes go down. The jellyfish and the whale come into that room with him: trim the strips level with the dome rim, hang the dome above his standing reach, and tape the whale flat to the wall with the string off it. Heat is the day's other hazard: water every half hour, shade by 11:00, hats outdoors, cream at eight and cream again at eleven, and everyone comes in if Azlyn goes quiet and flushed.

Day 211
The Tent Goes Up
The Big Book of Little Days · July · Week 30Day 210 · for the grown-up
July · Week 31

Camping Adventures ⛺

July 30 – August 5, 2027 · Days 211–217

Camp goes up in the yard on Friday and stays up until Thursday. A sheet over the clothesline, a ring of stones with a paper fire inside it, four bedrolls, and a flag she paints herself. Every day adds one piece and every piece stays outside, so the thing she walks out to on Thursday morning is one she has been living in for a week.

The week crosses from July into August and half of it runs on water: two bowls of dishwashing out by the tent, a soapy shower curtain down the lawn, a dish put out for the birds in the heat. Thursday is the big day. Everything still living indoors goes out to the tent in one morning, she finishes the camp, and the whole thing comes down after lunch while everybody still likes it. You spend Wednesday getting it ready, and Wednesday is the half she will ask to do again.

🧒 What Azlyn will learn
  • Pegs, weights and ties. What holds a sheet up in a breeze, and what lets it go.
  • A camp has an order. It goes up in a sequence, gets lived in, and comes down in that sequence backwards.
  • One symbol, one meaning. She paints a flag and then reads it from thirty feet away, which is the same trick letters run on.
  • Real kitchen work. Snapping beans, folding a foil seam, levelling off a cup, counting spoons out loud and starting again when she loses the number.
  • Staying still outdoors. Twenty minutes on her back naming what she can hear, which is harder for her than any of the building.
👶 KRESTON THIS WEEK

Kreston is 13 months this week. He walks, climbs anything knee-high and would rather carry something across the yard than sit down with it. He turns 14 months on Thursday the 5th, and brings scribbles, two blocks stacked, and three to five words you can make out.

The Big Book of Little Days · JulyWeek 31 · opener →
🌍 Around the world Week 31 · read it on Day 211

Norway: Allemannsretten ⛺

Norwegian law gives everybody the right to roam. Anyone can walk open country, swim in the lakes, pick berries and pitch a tent for a night on land they do not own, so long as they stay about five hundred feet from the nearest house and leave the ground as they found it.

✨
Try it

Make a matpakke, the Norwegian packed lunch: open sandwiches stacked with a square of parchment paper between each one and eaten outside. Azlyn builds the pile and wraps it.

The Big Book of Little Days · JulyWeek 31 · around the world →
Around the world w31-world.png
👩 What you'll learn
  • A space she can fit inside changes the way she plays in it
  • Fever makes children clingy, and meeting it is the fastest way through the day
  • Naming a sound is how she learns to pick it out of the rest
  • Summer needs less structure than you'd think
  • Symbols are a big abstraction, and flags are the easiest entry point
  • A list she can read herself puts her in charge of the packing
  • Big days are frequently too big, and the fix is leaving early
Did you know

Norwegian nurseries take the children out in every weather, and some spend the whole day outdoors.

Clearing the Ground

You need: 1 stiff yard broom · 1 bucket · 4 sticks or tent pegs.

  1. Walk the garden with her and let her choose where camp goes. Two things decide it: flat ground and shade by midday.
  2. Sweep the loose stuff into a pile and let her pick it into the bucket. Run your flat hand over the square afterwards for the stones she missed.
  3. Push a stick into each corner. That patch is camp now, and the sheet goes over it at quarter past nine.

The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

The Clothesline Tent

⏱️ 60 min🧰 8 items

You need: 1 old flat sheet or a double duvet cover, The clothesline, or rope tied between a fence and a tree, 8–10 clothespins, 6–8 stones, bricks or heavy books, 1 old towel or picnic blanket for the floor, String, 6 feet, 1 pair of adult scissors (adult only), The 4 corner sticks from this morning

  1. Throw the sheet over the line and slide it along until both sides hang the same.
  2. Clip the sheet to the line, one peg every hand's width, eight or ten in all. Every peg goes over line and sheet together.
  3. Weight both long edges from the outside with the stones, spaced along the hem so the walls hang straight. Nothing goes on the roof.
  4. Cut the string into four eighteen-inch lengths with your scissors and tie a corner at each end out to a corner stick, so both doorways stand open.
  5. Lay the towel or picnic blanket inside, corner to corner, and send her in.
  6. Have her crawl the length twice, in one door and out the other. Anything she brings down gets rebuilt before you call it finished.

💡Pitch it lower than you think you need to. A sheet at your shoulder sags to her head by lunchtime.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Firewood Walk

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take a bag to the hedge at the end of the road and gather sticks for a fire nobody will light. Dry ones, thumb-thick and shorter than her arm. Fifteen is enough, thirty is better. She carries the bag home.

Outdoors d211-outside.png

Second main event · 1:00–2:30 PM

The Paper Campfire

Camp needs a fire. Stones, sticks, torn paper and a flashlight, outside the tent door all week.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: The sticks from the walk, 10–15 stones for the ring, Red, orange and yellow paper (junk mail, a magazine, or a grocery bag torn into strips), Masking tape, 1 flashlight with fresh batteries, 1 empty tin or a small plastic tub to stand the flashlight in

  1. Lay the stones in a ring the size of a bike wheel, a long stride out from the tent door. She places every one.
  2. Stand three sticks against each other like a tripod and lean the rest around them. It falls over. Build it again and let her work out that the first three hold the rest up.
  3. Tear the paper into flames a hand long, twenty or so, and twist the bottom of each one into a stalk.
  4. Tape the stalks low on the sticks so the flames stand upright between them, red near the ground and yellow at the top. Tape paper to stick, never paper to paper.
  5. Stand the tin in the middle of the stack and drop the flashlight into it pointing straight up.
  6. Switch it on and kneel in the doorway to look at the fire from inside, where the shade lets the light show.
  7. Leave it built. At quarter past four, lift the flashlight out of the tin and take her into the tent with it, then untie the four corner strings so both doorways fall shut. A sheet with the doors down is as dark as July gets.

💡Give the fire one rule and hold it all week: the sticks stay inside the ring.

  • Sort the firewood into three piles by length and stop there.
  • Build the fire indoors on a tray and put the tent up tomorrow.
🌳 Out again · pick one
  • A friend's house, and take the flashlight, because she describes a tent better with a prop in her hand
  • Your own street at half past two, walking the shady side on purpose
  • The paddling pool in the yard, if leaving camp is more than anyone can face
  • The playground with the tunnel, which she will be calling a tent by now
Day 211 · For the grown-up The Tent Goes Up · Friday, July 30
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and walking. Give him one stick of his own, because holding something while moving is the job he is on now. He drops it, stops, picks it up and sets off again. That is the pace for the last hundred yards.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

At 13 months he climbs, and a knee-high ring of stones reads as an invitation. Give him two stones of his own, each wider than his fist and too big for his mouth, to carry from the wall to the ring and back. Sit him in the doorway with the flashlight switched off, then take it back before the fire goes together.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

A space she can fit inside changes the way she plays in it.

Azlyn has been climbing into cupboards and under the table since she was two, and a sheet over the clothesline gives her the same thing with a door on it. A small enclosure does two jobs at once. It cuts the amount of room her attention has to cover, so the play she starts in there runs longer and gets more complicated than the same play on open carpet. It also hands her a boundary she controls, which is why the first thing out of her mouth is who is allowed in. Children with a den of some kind take themselves back to it when they are tired or cross, and settle there before anyone suggests it.

⚠️

Safety: A clothesline sits at her neck height and a rope between two trees sits lower. The sheet stays on it all week, so peg something bright along any bare stretch she runs past. Kreston is 13 months, walks straight at anything new and pulls on it, so nothing heavy sits where it can come down on him. Every stone you hand him is wider than his own fist and too big for his mouth, and the ring stones stay in the ring. Weight the sheet from the outside and keep the roof clear. The build and the stick walk are both outdoors before noon, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you.

Snapping the Beans

You need: a bag of green beans · 2 bowls · 1 low step or upturned crate.

  1. Sit her on the step in the shade with the full bowl on her lap and the empty one beside her.
  2. Show her the snap once. Hold a bean at both ends, bend it until it goes, then break each half again.
  3. Leave her to it and go and get the foil out. The parcels need two handfuls at quarter past nine, and she will fill all four.

Dinner in a Foil Parcel

⏱️ 60 min🧰 8 items

You need: 1 roll kitchen foil, 4 potatoes, parboiled and cooled (adult, done the night before), Butter, Grated cheese, Green beans, zucchini, sweetcorn or whatever is in the fridge, 1 tablespoon, 1 permanent marker, 1 baking tray

  1. Tear four sheets of foil off the roll, each about the length of your forearm, and lay them flat on the tray and the table.
  2. One cold potato into the middle of each sheet. She squashes it flat with the back of the tablespoon.
  3. Load them together: a spoon of butter, a handful of grated cheese, her snapped beans, whatever else came out of the fridge.
  4. Fold. Bring the two long edges up to meet, fold them over each other twice, then fold each end up twice. She brings the edges together and you pinch the seams shut.
  5. Write a name on every parcel in marker. Hers, Kreston's, yours, Joseph's.
  6. Back on the tray, into the fridge, and into a hot oven at half past five for thirty minutes.

💡Shiny side in or out makes no difference. The seal does: a parcel folded flat at every edge steams the potato through, and one that gapes stays hard.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Chalking the Shade

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take the chalk out at half past ten and draw round the shadows: the tent, the fence post, the trash can, her own. Fat lines, and write the time inside one. Go back before dinner and find every shape sitting in the sun with its shadow moved. Bring the chalk out again for the redraw.

Rolling the Beds

Four bedrolls, one per person, tied and labeled. They stay rolled by the tent door until Thursday.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: 1 blanket or large towel per person, four in total, 4 pillows, String, cut into 8 lengths of eighteen inches, Thick card cut into 4 luggage labels, 1 hole punch, or scissors (adult only), 1 marker

  1. Blanket flat on the floor, pillow across one end, both long sides folded in over it so the roll ends up the width of the pillow.
  2. Roll from the pillow end, tight, kneeling on it as it goes to push the air out. She kneels, you roll, swap halfway.
  3. Two ties on each roll, a third of the way in from each end, knotted twice. Her finger holds the first knot while you pull the second.
  4. Punch a hole in the corner of each label. The punch is yours, or the scissors are, and they go back on the shelf after.
  5. She names each roll and you write it on the label in marker, then thread the label onto one of the ties.
  6. Stand all four on end by the tent door, then let her untie hers and lie down on it. Roll and tie it again together.

💡Tie them tighter than feels kind. A roll that sags apart the first time she lifts it gets abandoned by dinner.

  • The duck pond, closer, if the drive is more than today can carry

  • Home, the paddling pool, and nobody in the car at all
Day 212 · For the grown-up The Camp Kitchen · Saturday, July 31
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and carries things while he walks, so give him a fat piece of chalk and let him take it round the patio. He will not draw with it yet. He holds it, drops it, sits down on the line you chalked and slaps the ground flat-handed.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He walks now, and at the lakeshore he heads for the water without breaking stride, so he stays within arm's reach. Back at camp, hand him a folded towel to carry to the tent door and let him make the trip four times. At 13 months he would rather carry laundry than a toy.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Fever makes children clingy, and meeting it is the fastest way through the day.

August is the month somebody in the house goes down with something. Azlyn will want to be on you all day once she is running a temperature, and she drops the independence she had last week. That is her nervous system spending its energy on the infection and borrowing regulation from you. A fever runs its own course whatever anybody does, so what sits in your hands is how the hours feel while it runs. Carrying her makes them shorter for both of you, and pushing her back into a normal day buys an argument you lose. Cancel the day, keep the fluids coming, and let her lie on you.

⚠️

Safety: The oven is on and the parcels come out hot and full of steam, which scalds worse than the tray does. You open them, away from both children, and let them stand two minutes first. At the lakeshore Kreston is 13 months and walks straight at water, so he is within arm's reach the whole time. The shadow chalking and the lakeshore are both open sun, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors and the hole punch stay with you.
