Carrying the Day Outside

You need: 1 laundry basket · the old blanket · 2 cushions.

  1. Hand her the basket at the back door and tell her the whole day is going outside and staying there.
  2. She loads it and carries it out. Blanket first, then the cushions, then whatever else she decides the day needs. Two trips is fine and four is better.
  3. Spread the blanket in the deepest shade in the yard and leave it. That is the floor until dinner.

The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

Lying Down and Listening

⏱️ 60 min🧰 5 items

You need: 1 old blanket, 2 cushions, 1 pitcher of water and 3 lidded cups, A sun hat each, 1 paper bag for anything she picks up

  1. Blanket in full shade, cushions at one end, pitcher and cups where you can reach them lying down. Hats on before anybody lies back.
  2. Round one, eight minutes, eyes shut. Take turns naming one thing you can hear. A bee, a car, a door, the leaves. The long silences are where the small sounds arrive, so let them run.
  3. Round two, six minutes, eyes open and still flat on your back. Name what crosses the sky: a bird, a plane, a leaf going over, one cloud pushing past another.
  4. Round three, six minutes, palms and heels down on the ground beside the blanket. Grass, a root, a stone, a dry crumbling patch, an ant on her ankle. Anything she wants to keep goes in the paper bag.
  5. Pour a cup at every change of round whether she asks or not, and refill from the pitcher when it runs low.
  6. Twenty minutes covers all three rounds, and the rest of the hour is hers. The blanket, the shade and the water stay where they are, and she uses them however she likes.

💡You will want to fill the gaps. Sit in them. Count ten after each thing she names, and she fills the space herself.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Barefoot Lap

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Shoes and socks off at the back step, then walk the garden edge right round, twice. Grass in the shade, grass in the sun, the warm slab by the door, gravel, a drain cover, the cold patch under the tap. She names each one as she stands on it. The slab and the drain cover get the back of your hand first. Nobody puts shoes back on until lunch.

Outdoors d213-outside.png

What the Clouds Turned Into

Today you write the sky down. She lies back for a cloud, then comes up on her elbows to watch it become a drawing, six sheets or two.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: 6 sheets of paper, Crayons, 1 pencil, 1 hardback book or stiff card as a drawing board, Masking tape, 1 clothespin

  1. Tape a sheet of paper to the book so the breeze cannot lift it, and sit beside her with the pencil and the board on your knees.
  2. She lies back, calls a cloud and says what it is, then sits up next to you to watch it appear. You draw the thing she said rather than the thing you can see. A dog with eight legs is a dog with eight legs.
  3. Write her words along the bottom of the sheet, the ones she used, then tape on a fresh page. Six sheets, six clouds.
  4. Clip the finished pages to the corner of the blanket as they come off the board, or the first gust puts them over the fence.
  5. Hand her the crayons and let her fill in the sky round each shape while the next cloud arrives.
  6. On an empty blue afternoon she names what is moving instead: a bird, a plane, a bee, the top of the tree bending.
  7. Sit her up with the stack and let her read all six to Kreston, page by page, in her own words rather than the ones written down.

💡Draw a bad one and take your time over it. She corrects it, and the correcting tells you what she can see up there.

Day 213 · For the grown-up The Day Outside · Sunday, August 1
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and has walked most of his miles on carpet. Grass moves under him and tickles, and it stops him dead for a minute before he commits. Take his shoes off and set him down on the edge of the blanket. Let him choose when he steps off.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He goes in the stroller for the walk and out of it the moment there is grass. At 13 months he climbs every curb, every step and the low wall by the gate. Give him the wall for five minutes rather than lifting him past it. Water at every stop.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Naming a sound is how she learns to pick it out of the rest.

Lying still and saying a bee looks like nothing and is hard work for her. A garden hands Azlyn one wash of noise, and to name a bee in it she holds that one thread and lets the traffic, the leaves and her own breathing fall to the back. Small children get better at this with practice, and the practice needs somewhere quiet enough for the small sounds to arrive, which is what the gaps are for. Attaching a word to a sound makes it a thing she can find again tomorrow. Eyes shut helps, because nothing else is competing for her.

⚠️

Safety: The whole day runs outdoors, so the sun comes first: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven, blanket in full shade, water at every change of round. Walk the barefoot circuit yourself in shoes first and clear the glass, the dog mess and whatever the trash cans dropped. The paper bag of stones and grit stays up on the bench with you. Kreston is 13 months and puts everything he picks up into his mouth, so check his fists at every change of round and swap what you find for something too big to swallow.

Everything That Needs Washing

You need: 1 laundry basket · 1 damp cloth.

  1. Send her round camp with the basket for every cup, plate and spoon used since Friday.
  2. Wipe the worst off each one with the damp cloth at the back door, so nothing goes into the dishwashing with yesterday's cheese on it.
  3. Count the cups out loud into the basket. That number is hers for the morning.

The Camp Dishwashing Station

⏱️ 60 min🧰 9 items

You need: 2 dishpans or buckets, Warm water from the kettle, topped up cold, 1 squirt dish soap, 1 scrubbing brush and 1 sponge, 1 dish towel, 6 clothespins and a short line, 2 chairs to string the line between, The camp cups, plates and silverware, 1 low bench, upturned crate or step

  1. Bench in the shade, two bowls side by side. Fill the left from the kettle and top it up cold until you can hold your hand in it. Fill the right one cold.
  2. One squirt of dish soap into the left bowl only, and let her whisk up the foam with her arm in to the elbow.
  3. Brush for the plates, sponge for the cups. Left bowl first, then straight into the right one to rinse. She does every piece and you re-do the two that matter.
  4. Rinsed things stack on the bench to drip. She builds the stack.
  5. String the short line between two chairs, hand her the six clothespins, and peg up the dish towel and whatever else got wet.
  6. Tip both bowls out onto the grass the moment the last cup is done. She carries them in one at a time, empty.

💡Give her the left bowl and keep the tap and the kettle to yourself. Stopping her to top it up ends the job.

Water for the Birds

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Birds run short of water in early August. Stand a wide shallow dish or an upturned trash can lid in the shade, fill it a thumb deep, and put a flat stone in the middle for the smaller birds. She fills it, carries it and picks the spot.

The Soapy Slide

A shower curtain, two buckets and a squirt of dish soap turn the lawn into the thing she talks about for two weeks.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: 1 old shower curtain, tarpaulin or heavy plastic sheet (two split trash bags taped together works for a short one), 4 heavy stones or tent pegs for the corners, 2 buckets of water, 1 squirt dish soap, Towels, Swimsuits

  1. Walk the patch first with your hand and then your bare foot, feeling for stones and buried roots before anything goes down.
  2. Lay the sheet flat on level grass, well clear of the path, the step and the fence posts, and weight all four corners with the stones.
  3. Tip the first bucket down it from the top end, add the squirt of dish soap halfway along, and spread it with your hand.
  4. Swimsuits on. Show her the run-up once: three steps and sit down, feet first, head up. Sitting is the only landing.
  5. Second bucket over it whenever the middle goes dry, about every ten minutes in this heat.
  6. Stop before she is finished rather than after. Straight into a warm towel, and the swimsuit comes off out on the grass.
  7. Roll the sheet up away from the tent and stand it in the shade to dry.

💡More water and less soap. A second squirt turns the grass round the sheet into a skating rink for whoever walks past holding Kreston.

  • Wash the bikes and the trike with the leftover foam.

  • The duck pond, going late and taking rolled oats rather than bread
  • The riverside path for the shade and the breeze off the water
  • The splash pad, if there is one within a sensible drive
  • The garden again, with the sprinkler on low
Day 214 · For the grown-up Water at Camp · Monday, August 2
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and walks straight at water, so site the bird dish where you can see it. Give him his own, an inch in the bottom of a bucket and a cup, with you beside it. Pouring is the whole afternoon at his age, and he is never near it unsupervised.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He stays off the sheet. A 13-month-old on wet plastic goes down backwards and hits his head, so he gets the grass beside it and a bucket with an inch in it. At the pond he will walk in, so he holds a hand or he goes in the stroller.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Summer needs less structure than you'd think.

This week has a plan on every page, and the days that land best are the ones where you follow half of it. Long stretches of unbroken outdoor time do what a sequence of good activities cannot: she gets bored, stays bored, and then invents. The gap between running out of ideas and finding one is where her own play comes from, and an adult who fills it with a suggestion closes it. Children with long free afternoons build longer, more complicated play than those on a run of planned blocks. Put the water out and let the afternoon go where she takes it.

⚠️

Safety: Run your hand over the whole patch before the sheet goes down. A stone or a buried root under wet plastic is what turns a slide into a hospital trip. Lay it on flat grass, never near a path, a step or a fence post. Keep Kreston off the sheet and out of the bowls, and stay within arm's reach of him the whole time either bowl holds water. A 13-month-old drowns in the depth of a dishpan, so tip both out the moment you finish. Soap and water take the cream straight off, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven, and again before the sheet goes down.

What Our Camp Is Called

You need: 1 sheet of paper · crayons.

  1. Sit in the tent and ask what camp is called. Take the first answer, however daft, and say it back with camp in front of it.
  2. Ask what one picture would stand for it. A sun, a fish, a boat, the letter K. She picks.
  3. She draws it small five or six times while you watch. The fifth one goes on the flag at quarter past nine.

The Flag Over the Tent

⏱️ 60 min🧰 10 items

You need: 1 old white pillowcase, dish towel or plain t-shirt, Washable poster paint, 3 colors, 1 wide soft brush, 1 garden cane, bamboo pole, broom handle or a long straight stick, String, 3 feet, Masking tape, 1 jar of water and a wet washcloth, Newspaper to protect the ground, 1 pair of adult scissors (adult only), Her drawing from this morning

  1. Push a ball of masking tape onto the top end of the cane before you carry it out to her. Then newspaper down in the shade, pillowcase flat on top, and slide two more sheets inside it so the paint cannot come through to the back.
  2. Her drawing goes beside it as the reference. One symbol, and it wants to fill most of the cloth.
  3. Paint. The brush is wide on purpose and the jar of water sits between the three colors. The washcloth comes to her, not her to the tap.
  4. Leave it flat in the sun, which in this heat dries it in twenty minutes.
  5. Cut two short pieces off the string and tape a loop to each top corner of the flag. Nothing gets taped to the cane, because the flag has to travel up and down it this afternoon.
  6. Lash the pole to the fence post by the tent door with the rest of the string.

💡One symbol, and big. A flag with six things on it reads as a smudge from the other end of the garden.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Sign Hunt Down to the Pool

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Walk the route you take to swimming and count the signs: the red circle that means stop, the stick figure that means children, the arrow, the triangle on the recycling bin. She spots them and you say what each tells somebody who cannot read. Turn at the pool gates and walk back.

Flag Up, Flag Down

Three signals, two chalked stations and a bell. She runs the messages between them.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: The flag and its pole, 2 dish towels as hand flags, String, 6 feet, 2 clothespins to hold the flag at half height, Chalk to mark the two stations, 1 saucepan lid and 1 wooden spoon as the camp bell

  1. Chalk two circles twenty of her steps apart, camp at one end and the gate at the other.
  2. Agree three signals and no more. Flag at the top means come to camp, flag halfway means camp is shut, flag waved means dinner.
  3. Knot one end of the six-foot string through both corner loops, run it up over the taped ball on the end of the pole and down the far side, and pull the loose end to send the flag to the top. The two pegs pinch the string against the pole to hold it at half height for shut.
  4. She stands in the gate circle with her back to camp. One bang on the saucepan lid with the wooden spoon means look at the flag. She turns, reads it, does it.
  5. Swap. She works the string and the bell while you stand at the gate, and get it wrong on purpose twice so she has to correct you.
  6. Hand out the two dish towels as hand flags and send messages across the yard with nobody speaking, including you. Leave the flag at the top when you go swimming.

💡Three signals is the ceiling. Add a fourth and the whole thing turns into guessing.

Day 215 · For the grown-up The Camp Flag · Tuesday, August 3
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and walks, so let him do the first stretch on his feet with a finger to hold, then into the stroller. He points with his whole arm. Name the sign out loud when he aims at one, and keep walking.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He is 13 months and will go into the water off the side without checking whether anyone has hold of him. Arm's reach means the tiles as well as the water. Twenty-five minutes is plenty. Hold him under the arms and walk him along the shallow end so he does the stepping.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Symbols are a big abstraction, and flags are the easiest entry point.

The painted sun on that pillowcase is a mark standing in for an idea, which is the same trick as a letter standing in for a sound, and letters are eighteen months away. Azlyn can hold the flag version now because it is one picture with one meaning, chosen by her and visible from across the yard. Raising and lowering it adds a second layer: the same object saying two different things depending on where it sits. Every road sign she named this morning runs on that rule. She is doing the groundwork for reading in a form she can pick up and wave.

⚠️

Safety: A garden cane ends at the height of a running three-year-old's eye, so push the ball of masking tape onto the top end before the cane comes out to her, and lash the pole to the fence post so it cannot topple. Kreston is 13 months and will go into the pool without warning, so he is within arm's reach on the tiles and in the water. Painting and signal drills both run in the open: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven. The scissors stay with you, and the string comes off the pole at bedtime.

The Picture Packing List

⏱️ 60 min🧰 7 items

You need: Thick card cut into 12 strips, Crayons, 1 permanent marker, 1 rucksack or tote bag per person, four in all, The things still indoors: the flashlight, the cups, the sun hats, the water bottles, the sun cream, Masking tape, 1 bulldog clip

  1. Twelve strips in a row on the table. Name twelve things that have to go out to camp in the morning and let her do the naming, with you holding back the two she forgets.
  2. She draws one thing on each strip in crayon. A flashlight is a rectangle with lines coming out of it.
  3. You write the word underneath each drawing in marker, so anybody in the house can read her list.
  4. Loop a piece of masking tape onto the back of every strip and stick the row along the wall at her height, in the order things go into the bags.
  5. Fetch each thing off the shelf and pack against her list. She pulls a strip off the wall and lays it face down as each thing goes in.
  6. When the last strip is face down, clip all twelve together with the bulldog clip and hang it on her bag for the morning.

💡Let her pack her own bag and leave what she puts in it alone. A rucksack holding two teddies and one cup is one she carries the whole way tomorrow.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Where Everything Goes Tomorrow

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Walk out to the tent after the snack and stand in the doorway with her. She settles four things. The shade at eleven and the shade at three. The side of the door the water bowl stands on. The spot for the bench, set so nobody carries a full pitcher past the fire. The first thing out of the bags in the morning. You write none of it down, because she will remember.

The Camp Snack Bags

You make tomorrow's food this afternoon. Four tubs, three things in each, and she scoops and counts.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 7 items

You need: 4 small tubs or clean jam jars with lids, Cereal hoops, Raisins, Chopped dried apricot or dried apple, 1 tablespoon and 1 cup for scooping, 1 marker and 4 sticky labels, 1 tray to work on

  1. Tray on the table, four tubs in a row along it with the lids off and set aside.
  2. Cereal hoops first. One cup into each tub, and she levels the top of the cup off with her finger before it goes in.
  3. One tablespoon of raisins into each. She counts the spoons out loud and starts again if she loses count.
  4. One tablespoon of the chopped apricot into each, counted the same way.
  5. Lids on, and she presses every one until it clicks. Any tub that will not shut gets a spoonful taken back out.
  6. A sticky label on each lid. She writes her own name on hers however it comes out and you write the other three while she watches.
  7. Line all four up by the bags at the door. Kreston's is the one you chop into in the morning, not now.

💡Let her spill. A tray under the whole operation turns three spilt spoonfuls into something she tips back into the tub herself.

Day 216 · For the grown-up The Day Before · Wednesday, August 4
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 13 months and carries things while he walks, so give him one plastic cup and the job of getting it out to the tent door and back. He will take a route nobody else would choose. He understands bring it here about half the time.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Take him to the library and let him walk in on his own feet, which takes four minutes. At 13 months he pulls board books off the low shelf faster than anyone can put them back, so sit on the floor and let that shelf be his. Azlyn picks his book and carries it to the desk.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

A list she can read herself puts her in charge of the packing.

Twelve cards on the wall do a job Azlyn cannot do in her head yet. She can hold two or three steps at a time, and camp needs twelve, so the row of drawings carries the order for her and leaves her hands and her attention free for the packing itself. Turning each card face down as the thing goes in the bag is the part that earns its keep: she checks her own work and knows where she has got to without asking you. Small children finish more of a long task on their own from a list they can see than from the same list said out loud. She drew these, so they are hers to run.

⚠️

Safety: Raisins, dried apricot and cereal hoops are all the wrong size for a 13-month-old, so Kreston's portion gets chopped small in the morning and he does not get near the open tubs today. Loose food bags and plastic wrap go straight into the trash, not onto the floor where he is working. The planning stand at the tent door is twenty minutes of open sun, so hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven.

Everything in Three Trips

  1. Load the two baskets with everything the bags could not take.
  2. Three trips out to the tent and no more. Count them out loud.
  3. Put it all down in one heap on the grass beside the door. The rest of camp goes on at quarter past nine.

The Whole Camp in One Place

⏱️ 60 min🧰 10 items

You need: The tent, up since Friday, 6 spare clothespins, The bedrolls, four of them, The paper campfire and its ring of stones, The flag on its pole, 1 dishpan and 1 pitcher of water, 1 rug or picnic blanket, 6 heavy stones for the edges, 1 damp cloth, A sun hat each

  1. Hats on before anything else. Walk the tent with her first, both sides: every peg along the line, all four corner ties, every stone on the hem. She finds what a week of wind has shifted and puts it back, and a spare peg goes in wherever one has blown off.
  2. Six fresh stones along the two long edges from the outside, spaced so the walls hang straight. She knows this part and will tell you where you have it wrong.
  3. Rug down inside and wiped over with the damp cloth, then the four bedrolls along the back wall in the order she decides, labels facing out.
  4. Fire ring straightened out front, sticks stacked back into their tripod, any paper flame that has come off taped back on.
  5. Flag to the top of the pole, because camp is open. Then the cups, the snack tubs and the flashlight out of the bags and into the tent where she wants them, his tub chopped smaller than his fingernail first.
  6. Dishpan down at the tent door with the pitcher beside it. Then stand at the gate with her and look at the whole thing from thirty feet.

💡Move the rug rather than the tent. Shade crosses the floor by noon, and shifting what she sits on takes a minute where the sheet takes the morning.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Shady Loop Back to Camp

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Out early and short. Take the route that stays under trees, fill the bottles before you leave, and turn for home before eleven. Look for what else is sheltering: the dog under the bench, birds deep in the hedge, nobody on the field. Come back in through the front of the tent.

Striking Camp

Camp comes down on purpose, while everybody still likes it, in the order it went up.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: The whole camp, 2 laundry baskets or big bags, 1 dustpan and brush, or a stiff yard broom, 1 bag for the clothespins, 1 damp cloth, Your phone, for the photograph before it comes down

  1. Photograph it full first, with both of them inside it, before one thing moves. Take more than you need and take one from the gate.
  2. Flag down off the pole and she folds it corner to corner twice. The pole comes off the post and lies flat on the grass.
  3. Pegs off the line into the peg bag, six at a time so she can count them, then the sheet down and shaken.
  4. Bedrolls stay tied and go into the baskets with the rug on top.
  5. Carry the fire sticks back to the hedge they came from and tip them under it. The stones go back along the wall in a line.
  6. Wipe the bowl and the cups out with the damp cloth and carry them in.
  7. Sweep the ground flat until you cannot tell camp was there. She does the last of it on her own, then walks the empty patch.

💡Strike it an hour before anybody has had enough. Taking it down while it is still good is what makes her willing to put it up again.

Day 217 · For the grown-up The Big Camp Out · Thursday, August 5
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston turns 14 months today. He stacks two blocks now, so give him two of the fire stones, each wider than his fist, and let him try to put one on the other beside the ring. He has three to five words and one of them will come out today. Say happy fourteen months out loud to him, because nobody else is going to.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

At 14 months he wants to carry whatever everybody else is carrying, so give him the empty peg bag for the walk to the bakery. Your hand on the back of his neck says whether you keep going.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Big days are frequently too big, and the fix is leaving early.

The whole camp is up, everyone is enjoying it, and the temptation is to stay until somebody falls apart. Leave while it is still good instead, at the point where she would take another twenty minutes without argument. Small children remember the end of an experience out of all proportion to the rest, so an hour that finished well outranks three hours that ended in the grass screaming. You have watched this from the other side at every party she has ever been carried home from. Cutting a good day short by an hour is what makes her ask for the same thing again.

⚠️

Safety: A whole day outdoors in the first week of August is a sun day before it is a heat day: hat on, cream at eight, cream again at eleven, and once more after lunch. Shade over camp by eleven, and water every half hour. Kreston is 14 months and cannot tell you he is overheating, so watch for a hot dry neck, a red face and a sudden flop, and take him indoors to cool down. The dishpan at the tent door holds water only while somebody washes in it: stay within arm's reach of him while it stands full and tip it out over the grass the moment you finish. Raisins, cereal hoops and dried apricot are throat-sized at 14 months, so his tub gets chopped in the kitchen and the other three stay off the tent floor. Every stone you hand him is wider than his fist.
